 1 Task Description
 The interactive Result Viewer and the corresponding CADINP module RESULTS are post- processing tools for the finite element modules of SOFiSTiK with a CDBASE database (e.g. ASE, TALPA, MAXIMA, BEMESS, AQB, DYNA, HASE or HYDRA). The programs allow the graphical, tabular and diagram-representation of Information and Results saved in the Database. The data is roughly structured/ grouped as follows:
 • System
 - Cross-Sections and cross-sectional values
 - Groups
 - Loadcaseinformation
 - Structural Elements
 - Nodes
 - Finite Elements (BEAM,QUAD,BRIC..)
 • Results
 - Stresses on cross-sections
 - Group results
 - Loadcase results (e.g. Sum of support forces)
 - Nodal results (Displacements, Rotations..)
 - Element results
 • Design
 - Element results(utilisation, stresses, required reinforcement..)
 The Representaion depends on the type of result and can be selected as:
 • Graphical representation (Text, Vector..)
 • Table
 • Diagram
 The resulting Document consists of:
 • Page
 - Graphic
 2 Layer

From version 2022 we have moved a large part of the content to the new SOFiSTiK FEA manual.
 The new SOFiSTiK FEA Manual can be opened by following:
 https://www.sofistik.de/documentation/2025/en/fea/result_viewer/index_result_viewer.html
 Or you may also open the manual by following:
 Help Ribbon (SSD, Teddy, ...) → Online Help → FEA Manual
The modul results.exe has to be used for the batch start of Result Viewer via console. This modul is used automatically if it is running within the program WPS or SPS.
The input is done in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’Basics’).

The excerpt you provided is a master‐table from the SOFiSTiK “Result Viewer” input language.  It defines two broad classes of records—attribute records (which set drawing/listing parameters) and demand records (which actually request specific results to be produced).  Here is a structured breakdown of its contents:

1. Processing Model (Context)  
   • The Result Viewer reads one input block at a time until it encounters END.  
   • Within that block, “attribute records” immediately update internal parameters, but those changes are only visualized when a subsequent demand record or drawing command is issued.  
   • “Demand records” of type DSGN merely set attributes without triggering output—only non-DSGN demands generate tables or plots.  
   • The HEAD, PAGE and END records (not shown here) are described in the general SOFiSTiK basics manual.  
   • The DBO record (also elsewhere) determines whether results are treated as scalars, vectors or tensors.

2. Demand Records Section  
   These keywords tell the system what to list or draw:  
   • STRU  – Builds a table of structural elements: system values, user inputs, element numbering and designations.  
   • CROS  – Produces cross‐section tables: geometry, section properties and section results (stresses, forces).  
   • NODE  – Generates a nodal results table: displacements, support reactions and boundary forces.  
   • QUAD  – Lists element results for quadrilateral elements.  Depending on DBO, it can output scalars (e.g. bending moment), vectors (shear force or flow) or tensors (e.g. principal stresses, reinforcement).  
   • BEAM  – Tabulates 1D line‐element results (bending moments, axial and shear forces in frames and girders).  
   • BRIC  – Tabulates volume‐element (brick) results in 3D.

3. Attribute Records Section  
   These records customize the appearance and detail level of any subsequent tables or plots:  
   • DLIN   – Line style for drawing outlines and diagrams.  
   • ALIG   – Text or label alignment settings.  
   • VAL    – Controls printing of numeric values.  
   • DESC   – Toggles inclusion of descriptive text strings.  
   • DIAX   – Divider‐axis settings (e.g. for multi‐plot layouts).  
   • AXIS   – Axis scaling, orientation and labeling parameters.  
   • MODE   – Display mode (table vs. plot, 2D vs. 3D, etc.).  
   • TICK   – Tick‐mark spacing and style on axes.  
   • LABL   – Options for element or node labels.  
   • DLAB   – Detail labels (e.g. dimension or reinforcing‐bar tags).  
   (The full syntax and default values for each are given elsewhere in the manual.)

4. Record-Specific Parameter Blocks  
   Immediately below the attribute list the table shows which parameters apply to certain demand records—here illustrated for STRU and CROS:  
   • STRU:  
     – TYPE: Subset of element or system types to list (e.g. ALL, TRUSS, SHELL)  
     – ETYP: Element family codes  
     – REPR: Representation variant (e.g. outline, filled)  
     – FILL: Hatch or shading style for element displays  
     – UNIT: Unit override flag (e.g. kN vs. N)  
     – SCHH: Scale or hatch‐density factor  
   • CROS:  
     – TYPE: Section result type (e.g. stresses, stresses vs. location)  
     – ETYP: Element types whose sections are shown  
     – STYP: Cross-section family (I-section, pipe, etc.)  
     – REPR, FILL, UNIT, SCHH: Same roles as for STRU  

5. Usage Notes  
   • You can intermix attribute records in any order; they only take effect on the next demand.  
   • Multiple demand records can be combined into one listing or plot output—order among them is free.  
   • All tables and diagrams are finally drawn or written on the active BRIC output by default.  
   • To produce purely design‐checking output (no immediate drawing), issue the demand record with TYPE=DSGN.  

This structure allows you to finely control exactly which results you want (through the demand records) and how they should look (through the attribute records), all within one self‐contained input block.

The table is a registry of all “input records” that the SOFiSTiK Result Viewer can accept.  It is organized in two columns:

  •  Record  
     – The keyword that begins a new record in the input stream.  
  •  Items  
     – The list of fields (attributes) that may follow that keyword.  Whenever the Viewer reads a record of that type it will parse, update or buffer the values of these fields.

Below is a walk-through of the most important record groups and their parameters:

1.  Drawing-control records  
    •  CDB  
       – NO, TITL  
       (specifies the internal database number and the drawing title)  
    •  SIZE  
       – TYPE, SC, W, H, MARG, FORM, SPLI, SCAL, HLEG, WLEG, SLEG, LEGW, FREE, UMBR, SHAE, DATE, ASB, ARCH, DRUL, DRUR, DRUD, DRUU  
       (controls canvas size, margins, scaling, legend blocks, title block, date, orientation, etc.)  
    •  PICT AND FF  
       – M, W, H, MSCA, TITL, SPLT  
       (defines a picture frame with dimensions, scaling, title and split options)

2.  View-definition records  
    •  GRP VIEW  
       – NUMB, OPTI, ETYP, TYPE, X, Y, Z, ACHS  
       (creates a group or sub-view in the layout, positioned by coordinates X/Y/Z, with optional type code and axis flag)  
    •  LC  
       – NO, T, DESI, MAT, REF, NMAT, CS, XI, XIV, ENO, X, SECT, TITL  
       (defines a load case or a legend combo: number, title, material reference, cross-section name, etc.)

3.  Data-block and filtering records  
    •  DBO  
       – NAME, OPTI, UNIT, ND, POS, WIDT, SORT, REPE, FORM, BMIN, BMAX, TITL  
       (declares a data block to be retrieved—e.g. forces or stresses—with unit, node or element selection, column width, sorting, bounds and title)  
    •  FLT  
       – ID, NAME, RULE, ACT  
       (defines a filter by identifier, name and rule, with activation flag)  
    •  FILT  
       – NAME, TYPE, OPTI, VAL1, VAL2, EXRF  
       (an extended filter: by variable TYPE, option flags, value ranges and external-file references)  
    •  JOIN  
       – COL1, COL2  
       (joins two columns from different blocks or files into one combined series)  
    •  XLSX  
       – NAME, WS, ROW, COL, CLNM, TIME, CDB, ELEM, FILT, RESU  
       (imports results from an external Excel sheet: worksheet, row/column start, column names, timestamp, associated CDB number, element/ filter/ result codes)  
    •  TINF  
       – TYPE, MEDI, OPTI  
       (table info: media type, options for inclusion or exclusion in tables)

4.  Element-styling and color records  
    •  PFA / PLN / PMR  
       – ID1, ID2, ID3, ID4, COLO, R, G, B, A, TYPE, WIDT, SIZE  
       (these three records govern how lines, points and symbols appear: up to four selection keys, color index plus RGB(A) components, symbol type, line width or symbol size)

5.  Annotation and text-placement records  
    •  TXTP  
       – SHOW, OVLP  
       (controls whether text labels are shown and how to handle overlaps)

6.  Diagram and graph records  
    •  DIAG  
       – X, Y, GDEF, LCTP, YUP, LEGE, LBAX, SPPL, AXFU  
       (defines an X–Y diagram: axis limits, grid definition, caption type, unit/prefix formatting, legend, label axis position, subdivisions, arrow head size)  
    •  DGRA  
       – DESC, VAL1, VAL2  
       (adds a graphical element to the diagram with a description and two value parameters—typically for contour or shade boundaries)

General notes:  
– Records labeled HEAD, END and PAGE are not shown here; they control file headers, footers and page breaks and are documented in the SOFiSTiK “FEA/STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics” manual.  
– Whenever an “attribute record” (e.g. SIZE or PFA) is encountered, its fields update internal styling settings immediately, but these changes only take effect when the next list or drawing command (a “demand record” such as DBO, CROS, STRU, etc.) is executed.  
– Demand records themselves (e.g. STRU, CROS, NODE, QUAD, BEAM, BRIC) are not listed in this table; they are defined separately and primarily trigger data retrieval and rendering steps.  
– Shared field names (NAME, TYPE, OPTI, etc.) follow a consistent syntax: NAME is a user-defined label, TYPE/ETYP specify the category of element or result, OPTI flags optional behavior, VAL1/VAL2 set numeric limits or offsets, and COLO/R/G/B(A) control coloring.

Below is a structured walkthrough of the provided input table, its purpose and its contents. We first outline the overall context, then distinguish the two classes of records (attribute vs. demand), list the currently supported demand records with their meanings, and finally enumerate the attribute parameters that control their presentation.

1. Context and Processing Rules  
- The “Result Viewer” reads exactly one contiguous block of records, terminated by the keyword END.  
- Within this block, records fall into two categories:  
  • Attribute records: define or update display settings immediately upon reading, but only take effect when the next list or graphical output is produced.  
  • Demand records: request a particular type of result to be generated (tables, lists, drawings). They may also reset attributes if the special literal DSGN appears in the TYPE field.  
- RECORDS HEAD, END and PAGE are part of the general SOFiSTiK basic manual and are not detailed here.

2. Demand Records  
These instruct the viewer which kind of results to output. The table lists the following active TYPE codes (each generates its own display format):  
- STRU  
  Representation of structural elements. Outputs system values, input items, node/element numbering and designations in tabular form.  
- CROS  
  Outputs cross-section definitions, their geometric and material properties, plus computed stresses on those sections.  
- NODE  
  Generates a table of nodal results: displacements, support reactions, internal boundary forces.  
- QUAD  
  Produces a list format for quadrilateral finite elements. Can show scalar fields (moments), vectors (shear or flow), or tensor quantities (principal stresses, reinforcement).  
- BEAM  
  Tabular line representation for frame or girder systems (bending moments, shear forces, etc.).  
- BRIC  
  Tabular output for volume (brick) elements, typically stresses or other field results.  
- DLIN  
  (Not elaborated in this excerpt; presumed to handle line-based output formatting.)  
- ALIG  
  (Likely alignment control for lists or drawings.)  
- VAL, DESC, DIAX, AXIS, MODE, TICK, LABL, DLAB  
  (These are attribute records controlling label values, descriptions, axis modes, tick marks, etc., but are not demand records themselves.)

3. Attribute Parameters  
Following the demand-record definitions, the table lists the parameters that can be set for each demand type. Most appear twice—once for STRU and once for CROS—because each demand type has its own set of formatting options. The common attribute fields are:

• TYPE   : Specifies whether the record is a design setting (DSGN) or an actual demand.  
• ETYP   : Element type code to include or filter (e.g. BEAM, QUAD).  
• STYP   : Sub-type (where relevant).  
• REPR   : Representation style (table, list, graph).  
• FILL   : Fill pattern or shading for graphical outputs.  
• UNIT   : Unit system (e.g. kN, m, °C).  
• SCHH   : Scale or hatch pattern index.

4. Continuation Note  
The bottom line “Table continued on next page” indicates that further records or attribute details follow in the manual.

Summary  
This input table serves as both a catalog of result-type requests (STRU, CROS, NODE, etc.) and a menu of formatting attributes (TYPE, ETYP, REPR, etc.) that control how those results will be displayed in subsequent listings or drawings. Users define or modify attributes at any point, then invoke a demand record to produce output under those settings.

Below is a structured, record-by-record description of the table you provided, set into the wider RAG‐vector‐store context. The Result Viewer reads one block of input (terminated by “END”), in which attribute records update internal settings immediately but only take effect on the next listing or drawing. Demand records, on the other hand, request specific types of output. The four records shown in your snippet—NODE, BEAM, QUAD and BRIC—are all demand records that carry a fixed set of items (fields) to control what results get extracted and how they are formatted.

1.  Overview of Demand Records
    •  Demand records are lines whose first entry is one of the keywords below (NODE, BEAM, QUAD, BRIC).  
    •  Each demand record is followed by a sequence of positional parameters (called “Items”) that tell the viewer which results to list and in what style.  
    •  If the special literal TYPE=DSGN appears, only the attribute values (formatting, units, etc.) are assigned but no data is actually printed in that pass.  
    •  Attribute records (e.g. DLIN, ALIG, VAL, …) may intersperse anywhere but are consumed immediately; their effect shows only when the next demand record is processed.

2.  Table Description
    The table has two columns:  
      – “Record” names the demand‐record keyword.  
      – “Items” lists all the allowed parameters for that record, in the exact order they must appear.

    Record: NODE  
      •  TYPE  – Specifies which node‐based result to extract (e.g. displacements, support reactions).  
      •  TOTA  – Indicates whether to list total, incremental, or component values.  
      •  REPR  – Representation style (table layout, decimal places, column headings).  
      •  FILL  – Controls cell‐background filling (on/off, color index).  
      •  UNIT  – Primary unit system code (e.g. kN, mm).  
      •  UNI2  – Secondary or alternate unit code (optional).  
      •  SCHH  – Schedule or heading‐format code for the table.

    Record: BEAM  
      •  TYPE  – Choice of bending moment, shear force, torsion, etc., along beam elements.  
      •  STYP  – Subtype or detail‐level (e.g. major vs. minor axis bending).  
      •  REPR  – Table representation settings.  
      •  FILL  – Cell fill options.  
      •  UNIT  – Unit code for force/moment.  
      •  SCHH  – Schedule/heading style.

    Record: QUAD  
      •  TYPE  – Scalar, vector or tensor field on quadrilateral (membrane or shell) elements.  
      •  STYP  – Subtype (e.g. principal stresses, reinforcement ratios).  
      •  TOTA  – Switch between total result or per‐load‐case contribution.  
      •  AVER  – Option to display averaged values at nodes vs. raw Gauss‐point data.  
      •  REPR  – Layout and formatting instructions.  
      •  FILL  – Background‐filling parameters.  
      •  UNIT  – Engineering unit code.  
      •  SCHH  – Schedule/heading code.

    Record: BRIC  
      •  TYPE  – Choice of results on volume (brick) elements, such as stresses or strains.  
      •  STYP  – Subtype (e.g. principal vs. Cartesian).  
      •  TOTA  – Total vs. incremental output.  
      •  AVER  – Averaging across element Gauss points or faces.  
      •  REPR  – Representation mode for tables.  
      •  FILL  – Table‐cell fill options.  
      •  UNIT  – Desired unit system.  
      •  SCHH  – Schedule header style.

3.  How It Fits into RAG Vector Store Ingestion  
    •  Each demand record corresponds to a distinct result‐type collection.  
    •  The listed “Items” become metadata fields in your vector store schema, so that queries can filter, sort or group by, for example, UNIT or REPR.  
    •  Attribute records (not shown here) feed global parameters (e.g. axis orientation, offsets, label‐fonts).  
    •  A subsequent “LIST” or “DRAW” command triggers the viewer to gather numerical results and produce the tables per these settings.  
    •  Storing each demand record plus its populated fields as a single vector record allows downstream indexing and retrieval by element‐type, result‐type, unit, etc.

This detailed breakdown should help you map each table entry into your RAG vector‐store schema, ensuring that every “Item” becomes a retrievable attribute alongside the numerical results themselves.

Result Viewer processes only a single input block which is finished with END. The input is analysed in turn within this input block. In this case one must distinguish between attributes and demand records. Most of the input records are attribute records. The values of this records are updated immediatly. However, their effects become visible only in the next list or drawing. If the literal DSGN is given for TYPE in the demand records, only the attributes are set. Currently there are following demand records:
 STRU Representation of structural elements. System values, input items, numbering as well as designations will represented as table.
 CROS Representation of cross section and cross section values and results (stresses) on cross sections.
 NODE Representation of results in nodes (e.g. displacements, support reactions and boundary forces) as table.
 QUAD Representation of a scalar variable (e.g. moment), vector (e.g. shear force or flow) or tensor (e.g. principal stresses or reinforcements) for quadrilateral elements as list.
 BEAM Representation of a line representation for frame and girder systems (e.g. bending moments) as table.
 BRIC Representation of results at volume elements as table.

 The description of the various records follow.

The table under the “CDB” heading defines exactly two input‐block parameters for closing the current database and opening a new one. In a RAG/vector‐store context, you can think of this as the schema that tells your ingestion pipeline how to switch from one storage context to another without losing existing configuration settings (VIEW, GRP, BOX, etc.). Below is a breakdown of how the table is organized and what each field means:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—describe each parameter’s name, its semantic role, any expected data type or unit, and the default value used when you omit that parameter.  
   • Two rows enumerate the only two options you can specify for CDB: NO and TITL.  

2. Contextual Behavior  
   • When you invoke CDB, it implicitly closes the “current” database in your session and opens a new one defined by these inputs.  
   • If the new database has already been defined elsewhere by a previous TITL directive, you don’t have to restate its file path; you can simply reference it by number.  
   • All other session settings—views, grouping, box definitions, etc.—remain exactly as they were. This design makes side‐by‐side or sequential comparisons of multiple databases straightforward.  
   • In the context of a .results file (e.g. graphic output, lists, or diagrams), the database‐selection UI control is locked, since the file already specifies which database is in use.  

3. Column Details  
   • Item: the keyword you place in your input stream (either NO or TITL). This tells the parser which argument you are providing.  
   • Description: a human‐readable explanation of what each keyword does. For NO, it’s a numeric reference to an already‐known database. For TITL, it’s the literal path and file name.  
   • Unit: what kind of data the parser expects. A dash (—) means “unitless” or “integer reference.” LIT indicates a literal string (path).  
   • Default: the value assumed if you do not explicitly specify this item.  

4. Row‐by‐Row Breakdown  
   a) NO  
     – Description: “Reference number of the database.”  
       • If you pass 0, the system will reuse whatever database was open at the very start of the session.  
       • If you pass any other positive integer, it looks up a database previously registered under that index.  
     – Unit: none (just an integer index).  
     – Default: 1, meaning “by default, switch to database #1.”  

   b) TITL  
     – Description: “Path and name of the database.” This must be a valid file‐system path or URI where your database file resides.  
     – Unit: LIT, denoting a string literal, typically enclosed in quotes if your interface requires it.  
     – Default: “*” (an asterisk). In most implementations this wildcard means “use the path from the last TITL command previously issued,” so if you don’t change the filename, it stays pointing at whatever file you used before.  

5. Usage Example in Pseudocode  
   • To switch to database #2, already defined:  
     CDB  
       NO 2  
   • To open a brand‐new database at “/data/dbs/customer-db.db”:  
     CDB  
       TITL “/data/dbs/customer-db.db”  

By capturing these two parameters—NO for numeric reference and TITL for literal filename—the table provides a minimal yet powerful mechanism for managing multiple databases in one analytical session, while preserving your display and grouping settings across switches.

CDB
 The current database is closed and the new input database is opened with the input CDB. Only the reference number of the database has to be given in the case of previous definition of this database with TITL.
 The current settings, .e.g. VIEW, GRP or BOX, are not changed. Thus it is possible to compare databases with similar systems directly.
 The database selection for graphics, lists and diagrams cannot be changed via user interface. When a .results file containing such an input is opened, the selection field will be disabled.

The input table defines six layout parameters—TYPE, SC, W, H, MARG and FORM—each controlling how the drawing is scaled, sized and framed on the output medium. It is organized in four columns:  
  • Item: the keyword or parameter name.  
  • Description: a brief explanation of what the parameter does and its possible values.  
  • Unit: the data type or measurement unit expected.  
  • Default: the value assumed if the user does not supply one.  

1. TYPE (Unit: –/LIT, Default: WIN)  
   • Governs the paper format. A positive value selects a landscape orientation; a negative value yields portrait.  
   • Can implicitly pick from predefined formats (DIN, ANSI A–D, HP A–D, matrix/laser standards, etc.) via literal codes (for example “A” for ANSI A, “-URS” for portrait Report Browser).  
   • When omitted, the system uses the currently defined Windows printer format (WIN).  

2. SC (Unit: none, Default: –)  
   • Sets the drawing scale.  
     – “0” forces the drawing to fill the page at the largest feasible scale.  
     – A hyphen (“–”) tells the program to choose the best engineering scale (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, etc.) to maximize coverage.  
     – Explicit values (for example “*1.E+10”) override automatic scaling, if technically possible.  

3. W & H (Unit: cm, Default: –)  
   • W defines the paper width; H defines the paper height.  
   • When both are specified, TYPE and SC may be automatically adjusted to fit.  
   • If one dimension is set to zero, the program selects the matching paper size based on the provided scale; with one zeroed, scale can be inferred from the nonzero dimension.  

4. MARG (Unit: LIT, Default: FULL)  
   • Controls border drawing around the plotted area. Options:  
     – OFF: no border at all.  
     – NO: draws an inner border and scale only; W and H then specify the drawable area.  
     – YES: reserves a free margin (2 cm default, 0.5 cm if too small) around the plot.  
     – FULL: adds an extra cut line at the outer paper limits—useful for drum plotters.  

5. FORM (Unit: LIT, Default: *)  
   • Specifies the frame style around the plot:  
     – STAN: standard DIN frame.  
     – ZTVK: ZTVK-88 compliant title frame (two bands at top and bottom).  
     – URS: Report Browser framing rules.  
   • The default “*” inherits the form from the last setting or program context.

The table in question defines a set of “TYPE” codes (and their negative‐prefixed variants) that a user can supply to a drawing or plotting program in order to select a paper format, orientation and default printer characteristics.  It is meant to work in conjunction with the more general rules for SIZE, WIDTH (W), HEIGHT (H) and SCALE (SC) as outlined in the accompanying text.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and entries:

1. Overall Purpose  
   •  When the user supplies a TYPE code, the software automatically looks up the corresponding paper dimensions and orientation, and then chooses the largest feasible scale (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, etc.) unless an explicit SC is provided.  
   •  A leading minus sign (–) before TYPE switches the paper into portrait orientation; absence of minus defaults to landscape.  
   •  TYPE codes cover built‐in report formats, current Windows printer settings, ANSI sizes, Hewlett‐Packard special formats, matrix/laser printer defaults and extended matrix capabilities.

2. Default Report and Printer Formats  
   •  URS / –URS  
      – “Default Report Browser document format”  
      – Uses the program’s internal browser/report layout size.  
   •  WIN / –WIN  
      – “Format of the current WINDOWS printer.”  
      – If used interactively, picks whatever printer was most recently defined; non‐interactive use defaults to Windows’ system default printer.

3. ANSI Paper Sizes (U.S. Letter and Tabloid Series)  
   •  A / –A  
      – ANSI “Letter” (11″ × 8.5″)  
   •  B / –B  
      – ANSI “Tabloid” (17″ × 11″)  
   •  C / –C  
      – ANSI “Ledger” (22″ × 17″)  
   •  D / –D  
      – ANSI “D‐size” (34″ × 22″)

4. Hewlett-Packard Special Plotter Formats  
   •  HPA / –HPA  
      – Paper A: 259 × 199 mm  
   •  HPB / –HPB  
      – Paper B: 416 × 259 mm  
   •  HPC / –HPC  
      – Paper C: 529 × 378 mm  
   •  HPD / –HPD  
      – Paper D: 809 × 528 mm  
   •  HP4 / –HP4  
      – Paper 4: 276 × 193 mm  
   •  HP3 / –HP3  
      – Paper 3: 404 × 276 mm  
   •  HP2 / –HP2  
      – Paper 2: 564 × 366 mm  
   •  HP1 / –HP1  
      – Paper 1: 787 × 564 mm

5. Matrix and Laser Printer Defaults  
   •  MP / –MP  
      – “Matrix printer with 8″ × 12″ (200 × 287 mm) paper.”  
   •  LP / –LP  
      – “Laser printer with A4 paper (198.4 × 280 mm).”  
   •  MPW  
      – “Wider matrix printers with 14″ × 12″ paper.”  
     (No negative variant given—assumes default orientation.)

6. Notes on Margins, Legends and Headers  
   •  Right margin width may be adjusted via WLEG; bottom border is fixed at ~1 cm for HEAD lines.  
   •  Legend text lines are limited unless enlarged legends (HLEG for HEAD, SLEG for picture legend) are specified.  
   •  HLEG < 0 places the HEAD legend on the left; HLEG > 0 places it on the right (right‐side placement uses smaller text).  
   •  Using the ZTVK command forces a DIN A4 portrait drawing with dedicated top and bottom title bands.  Their heights are also governed by HLEG.  
   •  Coordinate axes, scale bar and sample‐line annotation are automatically placed inside the drawing frame, excluding the reserved header band areas.  

By selecting one of these TYPE codes, users avoid manually computing paper dimensions and let the program pick the optimal scale and orientation. If instead the user provides W, H and/or SC directly, the software will compute the best matching paper format internally but still conform to the same orientation and legend‐placement rules.

The table defines a set of layout parameters that control how a drawing is partitioned on the paper, how coordinate axes are drawn, and how legends and margins are handled. Each row lists: the parameter name (Item), a description, the physical or logical unit it uses (Unit), and the default value (Default). Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. SPLI (Unit: LIT, Default: 1*1)  
   • Purpose: Subdivides the paper into a grid of smaller “picture” cells.  
   • Behavior:  
     – height×width: fills shapes column by column.  
     – width×height: fills shapes row by row.  
   • Use case: Splitting a large drawing into a matrix of subplots.

2. SCAL (Unit: LIT, Default: – )  
   • Purpose: Controls which coordinate axes are drawn and how dimensional lines appear.  
   • Accepted values:  
     – “–” (dash): draw all three axes (X, Y, Z).  
     – “YZ”: draw only the Y- and Z-axes.  
     – “ZX”: draw only the Z- and X-axes.  
     – “XY”: draw only the X- and Y-axes.  
   • Implicitly sets the plot orientation and which plane is implied by the view.

3. HLEG (Unit: cm, Default: 1.0)  
   • “Height LEGend” under the plot.  
   • Space reserved below the drawing for a textual legend or HEAD lines.  
   • If set negative, places the legend on the left instead of below (for large formats).

4. WLEG (Unit: cm, Default: 0.0)  
   • “Width LEGend” reserved to the right of the plot for a custom legend.  
   • When non-zero, pushes the main plot area left to accommodate the legend panel.

5. SLEG (Unit: cm, Default: 2.0)  
   • “S”ection LEGend height: controls the height of each partial/secondary legend block.  
   • Useful when multiple result sets need separate legend sections.

6. LEGW (Unit: cm, Default: * [automatic])  
   • Total width of the legend block if it’s overlaid on the drawing.  
   • An asterisk (*) lets the program compute a fitting width based on content and margins.

7. FREE (Unit: cm, Default: * [automatic])  
   • Margin “FREE” region around the structure or drawing.  
   • Ensures no plot elements touch the boundaries; automatic if not explicitly set.

8. UMBR (Unit: LIT, Default: YES)  
   • Controls word-wrapping and line breaks in the picture legend.  
   • Options:  
     – NO: never break lines; legend text may overflow.  
     – YES: insert a break if a line is too long.  
     – SUPP: break at the next blank space only, truncating long words.  
     – SHOR: allow breaks within a word if needed.  
   • Default YES ensures readability by avoiding horizontal overflow.

Contextual Notes From “SIZE” Documentation  
• Paper format can be chosen via TYPE (e.g., A, B, C, D, HP-series, URS, WIN) or by explicit width (W) and height (H).  
• An automatically determined scale (SC) maximizes drawing size subject to engineering scales (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, …). SC=0 forces maximal filling.  
• When one of W/H is zero, the other dimension plus SC defines the sheet size.  
• Margins: right margin default defined by WLEG; bottom border (~1 cm) holds HEAD lines or result designations.  
• For very large formats, legends and titles may shift to the right-hand side and use smaller text.  
• ZTVK can generate an A4 title band at top and bottom, with heights controlled by HLEG. HEAD lines map to program structure metadata, results descriptors, and event or bar lines.

Taken together, these parameters give fine-grained control over how plots are arranged, annotated, and scaled on various paper formats—ensuring consistent presentation in the SOFiSTiK Result Browser and printed outputs.

Below is a breakdown of the “TYPE → paper‐format” table.  This description is intended for ingestion into a RAG-powered vector store, with explicit notes on columns, data types, semantics and usage.  

1. Table name  
   • PaperFormatCodes  

2. Purpose  
   • Defines all built-in paper‐size TYPE codes (with optional orientation flags) that a user may pass to the plotting/printing subsystem.  
   • Maps each TYPE code to a human‐readable name and the physical dimensions.  

3. Columns  

   1. format_code  
      – Type: string  
      – Definition: A short mnemonic used by the software to select a paper size.  
      – Examples: “URS”, “-URS”, “A”, “-A”, “HPC”, “MPW”  
      – Notes:  
         • A leading minus sign (e.g. “-A”) indicates portrait orientation; absence of “–“ selects landscape.  
         • Codes without paired “±” entries (e.g. “MPW”) only support a single orientation.  

   2. description  
      – Type: string  
      – Definition: A concise English phrase identifying the paper or printer type.  
      – Examples:  
         – “Default Report Browser document format”  
         – “Format of the current WINDOWS printer”  
         – “ANSI Paper B”  
         – “Matrix printer with 8 x 12 inch (200 x 287 mm)”  
      – Notes:  
         • May mention special behavior (e.g. for “WIN”: uses last interactive-session printer).  

   3. width  
      – Type: float  
      – Definition: Nominal short dimension of the paper.  
      – Units: See unit column.  
      – Examples: 11.0, 259.0, 8.5, 200.0  

   4. height  
      – Type: float  
      – Definition: Nominal long dimension of the paper.  
      – Units: See unit column.  
      – Examples: 8.5, 199.0, 12.0, 287.0  

   5. unit  
      – Type: enum {“inch”, “mm”}  
      – Definition: Unit of measure for width/height.  

4. Sample rows  

   1. format_code: “URS”  
      description: “Default Report Browser document format”  
      width: null, height: null, unit: null  
      • Dimensions are determined by the program’s default report‐browser settings.  

   2. format_code: “-URS”  
      description: “Default Report Browser document format (portrait)”  
      width: null, height: null, unit: null  

   3. format_code: “A”  
      description: “ANSI Paper A”  
      width: 11.0, height: 8.5, unit: “inch”  

   4. format_code: “-A”  
      description: “ANSI Paper A (portrait)”  
      width: 8.5, height: 11.0, unit: “inch”  

   5. format_code: “HPB”  
      description: “Hewlett Packard Paper B”  
      width: 416.0, height: 259.0, unit: “mm”  

   6. format_code: “MP”  
      description: “Matrix printer with 8 x 12 inch”  
      width: 200.0, height: 287.0, unit: “mm”  

   7. format_code: “LP”  
      description: “Laser printer with A4 paper”  
      width: 198.4, height: 280.0, unit: “mm”  

   8. format_code: “MPW”  
      description: “Wider Matrix printers with 14 x 12 inch paper”  
      width: 14.0, height: 12.0, unit: “inch”  

5. Context and Usage Notes  
   • Users may also bypass TYPE entirely by explicitly supplying width (W) and height (H).  
   • If W or H is zero, the software auto-selects the corresponding dimension to honor a given scale factor SC (or picks the largest possible scale if SC=0).  
   • The combination of TYPE, explicit W/H, and SC flags is orchestrated to produce the largest feasible drawing at an engineering-style scale (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, …).  
   • Portrait vs. landscape: prefixing TYPE with “–” flips orientation, but explicit W/H overrides it.  

6. Potential Vector-Store Fields for Retrieval  
   • format_code.keyword – exact lookups (e.g. user passes “A” or “-A”)  
   • description.text – fuzzy search (e.g. “Hewlett Packard B”)  
   • width, height, unit – numeric range queries (e.g. find all formats between 200 and 300 mm wide)  
   • orientation – derived Boolean (landscape by default, portrait if “–” present)  

With this structured description, a RAG system can index and retrieve paper‐format definitions, support user queries by code, name or dimension, and seamlessly integrate with the broader printing/plotting parameter set.

The table on view defines a set of configurable sheet-layout parameters for SOFISTIK’s drawing output. It appears in the context of earlier “SIZE” rules (TYPE, W, H, SC), margin definitions (WLEG, HLEG), and HEAD/SLEG legend settings. Each row lists:

• Description: what the parameter controls and any valid options  
• Unit: the expected input unit or literal type  
• Default: the value assumed when none is supplied  

Below is a detailed walkthrough of each entry:

1. SHAE  
   – Description: Controls whether “HEAD lines” (structure identification lines) appear in the sheet legend or picture legend.  
     • NO  – Suppress any HEAD-line output.  
     • YES – Include the structure line in the sheet legend, or when multiple databases are in use, place the full path as a literal.  
   – Unit: LIT (literal flag)  
   – Default: YES  

2. DATE  
   – Description: Toggles printing of the current date inside the sheet frame.  
     • NO  – Do not print date.  
     • YES – Insert the date.  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: YES  

3. ASB  
   – Description: ASB (Analysis Set Boundary) number to be printed.  
   – Unit: LIT12 (literal up to 12 characters)  
   – Default: – (none)  

4. ARCH  
   – Description: Archive number for referencing.  
   – Unit: LIT12  
   – Default: –  

5. DRUL  
   – Description: Width of the left print border (margin) in centimeters.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.5  

6. DRUR  
   – Description: Width of the right print border in cm.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.5  

7. DRUD  
   – Description: Height of the lower print border in cm.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.5  

8. DRUU

   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.5  

Usage Context  
• These parameters typically complement the paper-size logic (TYPE, W, H, SC) described under “SIZE.”

• ASB and ARCH let users encode project or archival identifiers with up to 12 characters.  
• DRUL/DRUR/DRUD/DRUU define uniform 0.5 cm margins by default; users can expand these to accommodate larger legends or title bands.  

Together, they give precise control over what metadata appears around the plotted drawing and how much white space is reserved for legends, headers and footers.

The input is a four-column reference table that documents a set of picture- and table-control items available in a report-generation environment.  It defines each item’s purpose, its acceptable values or options, its units (where applicable), and its default setting when none is explicitly provided.  This table is typically used in conjunction with commands such as SIZE, AND, FF, and PICT to fine-tune the appearance and behavior of generated tables and diagrams.  Below is a detailed description of its structure and contents:

1. Columns  
• Item  
  – A short alphanumeric code or keyword used to invoke or refer to the parameter.  
• Description  
  – A narrative explaining what the parameter controls, along with any recognized suboptions or special notes.  
• Unit  
  – The physical or logical unit in which the parameter’s value must be expressed (for example, “cm” for centimeters or “LIT” for literal text). A dash (“–”) indicates “not applicable.”  
• Default  
  – The value assumed if the user does not override the parameter.

2. Rows and Key Parameters  
• SC (“Scale”)  
  – Controls the overall scale factor of the picture, affecting all drawing layers uniformly.  
  – Recognized values include:  
    • 0 – “format filling,” which expands the drawing to fill the page format;  
    • DEFA – an automatically chosen “engineering scale” that best fits the page;  
    • *1.E+10 (or any explicit numeric scale) – fixes the scale at the stated magnitude.  
  – Unit: none. Default: none (user must supply or rely on DEFA).  

• W (“Picture width”) and H (“Picture height”)  
  – Define the absolute width (W) and height (H) of the picture in centimeters.  
  – If set to “DEFA,” the dimension is determined automatically from current page and margin settings.  
  – Unit: cm. Default: none (implicitly DEFA if not specified).  

• TITL (“Title”)  
  – A user-defined header line for the table or diagram.  
  – Supports placeholders—e.g. <LC>, <LS>, etc.—that the system will replace with context-sensitive text such as the currently selected load case, subcase, result type, etc.  
  – Unit: LIT (literal text). Default: none (the system will generate a generic title if left blank).  

• SPLT (“Split”)  
  – Determines whether a long table should be broken into multiple side-by-side columns.  
  – Options: NO (single column) or YES (automatic splitting).  
  – Unit: LIT. Default: NO.  

• BRTI (“Browser Title”)  
  – A user-specified string that appears as the title within the document browser or tree view.  
  – Unit: LIT. Default: none.  

3. Contextual Notes and Placeholders  
• Placeholders can be truncated by appending a length limit in parentheses, e.g. <LC>(10), ensuring that overly long case names do not exceed a fixed width.  
• If a placeholder corresponds to a result or load-case selection that is not in effect, it simply expands to empty text, avoiding awkward gaps in the title.  
• The parameters SC, W, and H only affect diagram objects and have no effect if the current object is interpreted strictly as a data table.  
• When a new picture or table command is issued (PICT), it inherits the size and scale settings from the immediately preceding picture unless explicitly overridden.  

In practice, this table serves as the definitive reference for anyone scripting or automating the layout of engineering diagrams and data tables, providing both the syntactic keywords and a concise explanation of their visual impact.

The table at hand serves as a concise reference for all of the “placeholder” tokens you can embed in titles (or captions) when producing tables and diagrams in the host application.  In practice, you supply a custom title string via the TITL item; wherever one of these tokens appears, it will be replaced at runtime by the corresponding selection description.  If a particular token does not apply to the current result set (for example, no beam‐section filter is active so <BS> would be empty), it simply vanishes, and—if you’ve provided no explicit text—the system falls back on its built-in default title.

Structure of the Table  
– Two columns:  
  • Placeholder – the exact text to write in your TITL string (e.g. “<LC>”)  
  • Description – a human‐readable summary of what will be substituted  

Entries  
1. <FLT>  
   • Description: Inserts a marker if at least one filter is active. Use this to flag that results have been filtered.  

2. <LC>  
   • Description: Substitutes the list of currently selected load cases.  

3. <CS>  
   • Description: Shows which cross-sectional profiles have been chosen.  

4. <DC>  
   • Description: Displays the selected design cases.  

5. <BS>  
   • Description: Inserts the currently selected beam sections.  

6. <STAGES>  
   • Description: Names the construction stage(s) you have activated.  

7. <XI>  
   • Description: Adds the selected XI (internal identifier or combination index).  

8. <SEL>  
   • Description: A shorthand macro that expands to a sequence of <LC> <CS> <DC> <BS> <STAGES> <XI>, in that order. Useful when you want one token to pull in all primary selection settings at once.  

9. <GRP>  
   • Description: Inserts the current group selection. This is typically used when you have organized elements into named groups.  

10. <RESULT>  
    • Description: Embeds the list of selected results (e.g. “bending moment,” “shear force,” etc.).  

Additional Notes  
• Truncation: You can limit how many characters are printed for any placeholder by appending a length in parentheses, for example <LC>(10). If the expanded text exceeds this length, the last three characters are replaced with an ellipsis (“…”).  
• Default Behavior: If you omit a custom TITL or leave it blank, the system generates a generic title based on the result type. Placeholders that resolve to empty text are simply omitted—no extra spaces or separators are inserted automatically.  
• Pictures vs. Tables: The PICT, SIZE, AND, FF commands control picture sizing and framing but do not affect table layouts. When you start a new PICT block, all pictorial settings reset unless explicitly overridden. Tables, by contrast, inherit their width entirely from the system box and its framing borders.  

By referring to this table, you can craft dynamic, context‐aware titles that automatically reflect the user’s current selection of load cases, sections, design cases, and more—ensuring clarity and consistency across all exported diagrams and tabular reports.

See also: SIZE, AND, FF
 PICT
 A new table or new picture is started.
 The geometric picture definition W, H and the scale definition SC have no effect on tables.
 The current picture obtains from the previous picture all settings like size and scale.
 The scale which is calculated for the picture depends on the size of the structure box (system box) and the width of the borders around this box.
 The title of tables and diagrams can be set using the item TITL. Several placeholders can be used (see below). The placeholders will be replaced by the program.
 Remarks:
 • A placeholder will extend to an empty text if the current result selection does not require the selection represented by the placeholder.
 • The maximum length of the inserted text can be limited by specifying the maximum number of characters in brackets after the placeholder. E.g. <LC>(10) will truncate the inserted information about the loadcase selection after 10 characters where the last 3 will be used for printing ...
 If no text is specified, the default title will be printed.
 Available placeholders:
 Selected results

The input “Tables” specification is really a compact, four‐column reference table that tells the RAG importer how to group, order, and paginate geometry‐based records in your source file.  Below is a detailed, column-by-column and rule-by-rule breakdown of that table, including the related keywords SIZE, PICT, FF and the special conjunction AND.

1. Column Layout  
   • Item  
     – Name of the record or directive (e.g. STRU, CROS, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, BRIC, AND, SIZE, PICT, FF)  
   • Description  
     – A brief English summary of what that item does or how it affects grouping/drawing.  
   • Unit  
     – Typically empty for these control records (they don’t carry a “physical” unit) but still present for consistency.  
   • Default  
     – States whether the item is “on” by default or if there is no default (in practice, most of these are implicit unless overridden).  

2. Grouping Rules for Geometry Records  
   – STRU, CROS, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, BRIC  
     • Whenever you issue one or more of these records in succession—with no intervening items—their resulting data are merged into a single list in the output table.  
     • If you switch from, say, NODE → QUAD → NODE, you will end up with two separate lists: all the NODE entries before the first QUAD in list 1, the QUAD entries in list 2, and the second batch of NODE entries in list 3.  
     • Example from the source:  
       • Input:  
         NODE UZ REPR DLST;  
         QUAD MX STYP ELEM;  
         NODE SZ;  
         QUAD N STYP ELEM  
       • Output: two lists—List 1 containing the first‐and‐third NODEs, List 2 containing both QUADs.  

3. The AND Conjunction  
   – If you insert an AND record between two groups, the importer does *not* start a brand‐new table. Instead:  
     • It appends the second group to the first group in a *single* combined table.  
     • Useful when you want to preserve ordering or layering but keep the entire dataset in one composite table.  

4. Page‐Break Controls  
   – SIZE or FF (form‐feed)  
     • Instructs the importer to break the output table at that point and start a fresh page (or section).  
     • Neither SIZE nor FF carries a “unit” in this context—they function as flags.  

5. Graphics Layering Notes  
   – When you do *not* use AND between two drawing records, each new record block begins its own fresh drawing canvas in the output.  
   – If you *do* use AND, you are effectively saying “draw the next block in the same picture, on a new layer,” preserving the existing scale and view.  

6. “See Also” Cross-References  
   – SIZE, PICT, FF  
     • SIZE: also controls page break but can carry numeric values (e.g. paper size) in some dialects.  
     • PICT: generally signals insertion of an external picture or background image.  
     • FF: explicit form‐feed, guaranteed to start a new page or output section.  

7. Putting It All Together  
   By laying these records out in that four-column table, the RAG vector importer has a concise rule set for:  
   • Which geometric entities merge into one table,  
   • When to split into separate lists or pages,  
   • How to treat supplemental directives (AND, SIZE, PICT, FF),  
   • And how to manage drawing order and layering without disturbing scale.  

Every time you author or parse an input file, you consult this reference table: look up the Item (first column), read its Description (second column), ignore Unit if blank (third column), note whether it’s Default-on or off (fourth column), and then apply the combination, pagination, or layering rule as stated.

The table in question defines the input parameters for the “GRP” command, which controls how element groups (and secondary groups) are selected and represented in a report.  Below is a structured breakdown of each column and row, suitable for ingestion into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store.  

1. Columns  
   • Item (string key)  
     – The name of the parameter. Used as the primary identifier.  
   • Description (text)  
     – A human-readable explanation of what the parameter does. May include sub-entries.  
   • Unit (string or literal)  
     – The data type or measurement unit expected. “LIT” indicates a literal choice. A dash (“–”) indicates “no unit.”  
   • Default (string)  
     – The value assumed if the user omits this parameter.  

2. Context and Usage  
   • GRP is invoked when the user wants to selectively display or suppress element groups in an output report. If no GRP input is given, all element groups and types are processed by default.  
   • Internally, each element belongs to a group whose number = floor(element_number ÷ GDIV). GDIV is a system constant stored in the database (see program SOFIMSHC, record SYST).  
   • By specifying “ETYP” (element type), the user can override the numeric grouping and pick out only elements of certain types. Multiple ETYP entries may be combined in one GRP invocation.  

3. Detailed Row Descriptions  

— NUMB  
   • Description: “Group number (no definition = all)”  
     – If omitted, every group is included. If specified, only the matching group (integer) is processed.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: –  

— OPTI  
   • Description: “Option” with two legal values:  
     – NO: The group is not represented (i.e., it is suppressed).  
     – YES: The group is represented (i.e., it is shown).  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: YES  

— ETYP  
   • Description: “Element type”  
     – A literal code identifying which element class to include. If ETYP is used, only the listed types (regardless of NUMB) will be processed. You can repeat ETYP lines to include multiple types.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: –  
   • Allowed Values and Meanings:  
     - BEAM  – Beam elements  
     - SPRI  – Spring elements  
     - BOUN  – Boundary elements  
     - TRUS  – Truss elements  
     - CABL  – Cable elements  
     - TUBE  – Tube elements  
     - QUAD  – Plane (quadrilateral) elements  
     - BRIC  – Volume (brick) elements  

4. How to Index for RAG  
   • Parameter name → embedding key  
   • Description text → context field  
   • Unit and Default → structured metadata  
   • Enumerated sub-values (especially for OPTI and ETYP) → separate micro-documents or nested fields, ensuring efficient retrieval when the user queries “which element types are valid?” or “what happens if OPTI=NO?”  

5. Example Usage Patterns  
   • Select only group 3 and suppress it:  
     { NUMB=3; OPTI=NO }  
   • Show all beam and truss elements across every group:  
     { ETYP=BEAM; ETYP=TRUS }  

By decomposing the table in this way—explicitly naming each field, describing its behavior, listing data types and defaults, and capturing enumerated values—you create a clear, self-contained schema that can readily be turned into embeddings for a RAG vector store.

See also: SIZE, AND, PICT
 FF
 Item Description Unit Default
 A formfeed is forced. Normally the Report Browser decides, when a picture does not fit on a page any more.
 GRP – Selection of Element Groups and Secondary Groups

The input table defines three parameters used by the “LC” command (Load Case selection) when generating drawings or reports. It specifies, for each parameter, the name (Item), its purpose (Description), the measurement unit (Unit) and the default setting (Default). Together, these parameters control which load cases, transient times, or design cases are fetched from the internal result database for representation.

1. Common structure  
- Columns:
  • Item: the keyword to be supplied on the LC command line  
  • Description: semantic rules and special values  
  • Unit: the data type or unit designation (often “–/LIT” for literal keywords)  
  • Default: the value used if the parameter is omitted  

2. NO (Load-Case Number)  
Description  
• Selects the load case(s) whose results will be represented in the subsequent drawings or output lists.  
• If you supply a non-negative integer (≥ 0), that exact load-case index is used.  
• A negative integer (< 0) causes the system to pick the corresponding entry from the predefined load-case list.  
• Several literal keywords are also supported:  
  – DEFA: alias for FIRS (default behavior, see below)  
  – FIRS: choose the first load case in the list  
  – LAST: choose the last load case in the list  
  – NEXT: choose the next load case (relative to the last used)  
  – PREV: choose the previous load case  
  – ALL: include all load cases in the list  
  – NAME: look up a case by its title (TITL); warn if not found exactly  
  – FIND: same as NAME but silent on mismatches  
Unit  
  –/LIT (literal keyword or integer)  
Default  
  DEFA  

3. T (Time for Transient Results)  
Description  
• Specifies the time value at which transient (time-dependent) results are extracted.  
• Except for the NAME/FIND keywords, any valid input here behaves exactly like the NO parameter (i.e. indexing into the time steps as if they were “load cases”).  
Unit  
  sec/LIT (seconds or literal keywords)  
Default  
  LAST  

4. DESI (Design-Case Number)  
Description  
• Chooses which design case to use when displaying design-specific results such as reinforcement layouts or design stress envelopes.  
• Internally it parallels the NO parameter’s indexing rules (including literal keywords NAME and FIND), but applies them to the design-case data sets generated by BEMESS (reinforcements, design stresses) or beam-stress modules (AQB).  
Unit  
  –/LIT (literal keyword or integer)  
Default  
  DEFA  

Additional Context  
- Items MAT, REF, NMAT and CS are reserved but not yet implemented.  
- All results that have been stored “per load case” are referenced via NO. Design results (reinforcements, design stresses, beam stresses from AQB) are referenced via DESI.  
- Beam-section results (e.g. stresses) can further be refined by supplying ENO (element number) and X (section coordinate) to pick a specific cross section.  
- You can request multiple load or design cases in one call by listing numbers or ranges. For example:  
  • LC NO 1,2,3,4,5  
  • LC NO (1 5 1)  —interprets as “from 1 to 5 in steps of 1.”

Below is a structured, column-by-column walkthrough of the “LC” (Load Case) table as you would capture it for a RAG‐indexed vector store.  We describe each field, its role and allowable values, and then put it in the broader context of how load cases and design load cases drive results selection in your workflow.

1. Table Structure  
   • Each row defines one LC sub‐parameter (or “sub-keyword”).  
   • Columns are:  
     – Keyword (the literal text you type)  
     – Arguments / Syntax  
     – Data Type / Range  
     – Default or Not-Used flag  
     – Description / Notes  

2. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
   
   A. LC NO  
   • Syntax: “LC NO n1,n2,…,nk” or “LC NO (i j k)”  
   • Type: Integer list or range specification  
   • Range: Any positive integer representing a load or design‐load case index  
   • Default:  –  
   • Description:  
     • Selects which load or design‐load cases to include in the output list.  
     • You may enumerate discrete cases (e.g. 1,2,3,4,5) or specify a range with optional step (e.g. (1 5 1) for cases 1 through 5 in steps of 1).  
     • All “non-design” results (standard beam stresses, deflections, etc.) are fetched by referencing NO.  
   
   B. LC ENO  
   • Syntax: “LC ENO x”  
   • Type: Integer  
   • Range: 1…N  (where N is the number of defined beam cross-sections)  
   • Default: current beam section of active load case  
   • Description:  
     • Filters results stored per beam section.  
     • When multiple cross-sections have been stored for a given load case, ENO picks out exactly which section to retrieve.  
   
   C. LC T  
   • Syntax: “LC T …”  
   • Type: not yet used  
   • Range: —  
   • Default: —  
   • Description: reserved for future use (e.g. temperature‐dependent loads).  
   
   D. LC MAT  
   • Syntax: “LC MAT …”  
   • Type: not yet used  
   • Range: —  
   • Default: —  
   • Description: placeholder for material-specific load filtering or assignment.  
   
   E. LC REF  
   • Syntax: “LC REF …”  
   • Type: not yet used  
   • Range: —  
   • Default: —  
   • Description: reserved for selecting results by reference number (e.g. referencing an earlier result set).  
   
   F. LC NMAT  
   • Syntax: “LC NMAT …”  
   • Type: not yet used  
   • Range: —  
   • Default: —  
   • Description: future extension for “new material” or damage indices.  
   
   G. LC CS  
   • Syntax: “LC CS …”  
   • Type: not yet used  
   • Range: —  
   • Default: —  
   • Description: reserved for cross-section grouping or composite section identifiers.  

3. Contextual Notes  
   • NODE, BEAM, QUAD  
     – These keywords define the geometric entities on which results (loads, stresses) are stored.  They are independent of LC but used in the same REPR DLST listing.  
   • Design Load Cases vs. Regular Load Cases  
     – When you input a “design load case” index under LC NO, the system will pull reinforcement data, design stresses from BEMESS, and beam stresses from AQB.  
     – All other results (e.g. basic stresses, deflections, reaction forces) remain tied to ordinary load cases and are fetched via LC NO unless overridden.  
   • Multi-case & Multi-section Output  
     – The REPR DLST command can output multiple load or design cases and/or multiple beam cross-sections in one table.  
     – Just list all desired cases or ranges after “LC NO,” and list sections after “LC ENO” if needed.  
   • How the Table Drives RAG Indexing  
     – Each LC sub-keyword can be turned into a distinct node in your vector store.  
     – “LC NO” rows cover the majority of user queries about which load cases to retrieve.  
     – “LC ENO” addresses queries about beam cross-section selection within those cases.  
     – The unused fields (T, MAT, REF, NMAT, CS) can remain as placeholders, ensuring future compatibility without polluting the index with stale values.  

This breakdown should enable you to embed every column and row of the LC table into your vector store—tagging each sub-keyword by its syntax, expected argument types, usage patterns, and relationship to broader node/beam/quad result retrieval.

The table defines six optional “input” fields that control how element results (stresses, materials, etc.) are represented in output lists.  Each field has an identifier (Item), a concise purpose (Description), the expected input type or unit (Unit), and a default value (Default).  These inputs are most often used in combination with the load‐case selector (LC NO/LC DLST) or the beam/quad selectors (ENO/X) to produce customized result reports.  See also NODE, BEAM, QUAD for element‐type context.  

1.  MAT (Material selection)  
   •  Purpose: Choose which material (or stress‐point literal) to use when representing composite results.  If multiple materials or stress points exist, MAT lets you pick an aggregate value.  
   •  Equivalence: Any numeric MAT input behaves like the load‐case number selector NO.  
   •  AQUA stress‐point literals:  
     – ‘_MID’ average value  
     – ‘_MAX’ maximum value  
     – ‘_MIN’ minimum value  
     – ‘_AMX’ absolute maximum value  
     – ‘_AMN’ absolute minimum value  
     – ‘_LST’ last computed value  
   •  Unit: –/LIT  
   •  Default: DEFA  

2.  REF (Reference material)  
   •  Purpose: Specify an auxiliary or comparison material index, in addition to MAT.  Often used for ratio or difference plots.  
   •  Unit: –  
   •  Default: – (none)  

3.  NMAT (Nonlinear‐law material)  
   •  Purpose: Select which material law to use when reporting nonlinear results produced by TALPA/ASE.  Allows you to switch between different constitutive laws or model parameters.  
   •  Equivalence: Functions the same way as MAT for nonlinear output.  
   •  Unit: –/LIT  
   •  Default: STAN  

4.  CS (Construction stage)  
   •  Purpose: Identify the construction or erection stage index whose partial‐stage results you want to display.  Useful in staged‐construction analyses.  
   •  Unit: –  
   •  Default: 0  

5.  XI (Layer‐depth selector for QUAD stresses)  
   •  Purpose: Determine the vertical position within a QUAD element (e.g. shell or layered element) at which stresses are extracted.  
   •  Options (case‐sensitive strings):  
     – FAC: fraction of thickness from upper face (–1) to lower face (+1)  
     – TH: thickness‐coordinate measured from lower face upward (meters)  
     – THD: thickness‐coordinate from upper face downward (meters)  
     – TM: thickness‐coordinate from mid‐thickness toward lower face (meters)  
     – TMU: thickness‐coordinate from mid‐thickness toward upper face (meters)  
     – ALL: report results for all layers  
   •  Unit: LIT  
   •  Default: FAC  

6.  XIV (Absolute layer depth)  
   •  Purpose: Provide a numeric depth (in meters) for layer‐specific QUAD result extraction.  Only used when XI = TH, THD, TM or TMU.  
   •  Unit: –/m  
   •  Default: 0.0  

Additional context:  
–  None of these fields produce a new load case; they refine how already‐computed results are referenced.  
–  Load‐case (LC) input drives whether you see envelope, design, or history cases—these MAT/REF/NMAT/CS/XI/XIV fields then tailor material and depth choices within that case.  
–  You can output multiple cases or sections at once (e.g. “LC NO 1,2,3,4,5” or “LC NO (1 5 1)”), and these item settings apply per‐case.  
–  Although “T” also appears in related tables, the column T is not used here.  
This structured metadata ensures your vector‐store RAG system can reliably index and retrieve queries about material selections, layered‐element stress extraction, and staged‐construction reporting.

sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
Below is a concise, yet detailed, description of the “LC” (load case) input‐table, suitable for RAG vector‐store ingestion.  Wherever possible we’ve mapped each column to its purpose, noted dependencies on the surrounding system, and illustrated usage with examples.

1. Table Purpose  
   • LC selects which load, design, or history cases—and (optionally) which beam cross section—to represent in an output listing.  
   • Any results in the database that were stored “per load case” will be filtered by the LC input.  
   • Design‐case–specific results (reinforcements, BEMESS stresses, AQB beam stresses) also use the LC input; all other load‐case–based results use the NO field.

2. Cross‐References  
   • See also the analogous commands: NODE (node results), BEAM (beam‐element results), QUAD (quadrilateral‐element results).  
   • Combined‐output command: REPR DLST (can emit multiple cases or sections in one report).

3. Column Layout  
   The table is organized into these columns (left to right):

   – Keyword  
   – Field name  
   – Argument form/selection  
   – Mandatory?  
   – Data type  
   – Meaning

4. Fields in “LC”  
   • NO  
     – Selection: comma‐separated list of case numbers, or a generation block in parentheses.  
     – Mandatory: YES  
     – Type: integer list or ( start end step )  
     – Meaning: Specifies exactly which load/design/history cases to include.  
       • Example 1: “LC NO 1,2,3,4,5” produces cases 1→5 in the report.  
       • Example 2: “LC NO (1 5 1)” is equivalent—start=1, end=5, step=1.

   • X  
     – Selection: single integer or blank  
     – Mandatory: NO  
     – Type: integer  
     – Meaning: Selects a specific beam cross section within each chosen load case.  If omitted, all sections are reported.

   • T, MAT, REF, NMAT, CS  
     – Selection: (present in table but) NOT USED  
     – Mandatory: NO  
     – Type: —  
     – Meaning: Reserved for future extensions—currently have no effect.

5. Interaction Notes  
   • “LC NO” drives the retrieval of most “load‐case” results.  
   • If you specify a design load case, then reinforcements and stresses computed by external programs (BEMESS for design stresses, AQB for beam stresses) will also be displayed using that design‐case index.  
   • To narrow results to a beam cross section, pair LC NO with X (section number).  
   • You may list multiple LC commands in a single REPR DLST call to compare cases side by side.

6. Sample Usage  
   1) Output load cases 2, 4, and 7 for all beam sections:  
      LC NO 2,4,7  
   2) Output all sections of cases 1→3:  
      LC NO (1 3 1)  
   3) Output only section 5 of case 10:  
      LC NO 10 X 5  

This table lets downstream RAG queries slice the stored finite‐element results by load/design scenario (and optionally by beam section), enabling flexible, multi‐case comparisons in a single pass.

sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
The table under discussion defines six primary input keys that control which load‐case or design‐case results are retrieved and how they are presented when working with beam‐stresses output routines (AQB), cross‐section queries, legends, and history cases.  All inputs (except for the special NAME/FIND variants) are equivalent to the generic “NO” parameter that names a load- or design-case.  In practice, these fields let you select the case number or position (and, in one instance, a cut position) to extract stresses, forces, or other derived quantities from the model database.

1. ENO  
   • Description: “Beam number for stresses from program AQB.”  
     – Specifies which beam (by its numeric identifier) to interrogate for line‐based stress results.  
     – Except for NAME/FIND, ENO behaves exactly like NO (the standard load‐case selector).  
   • Unit: –/LIT (no physical unit; literal integer input)  
   • Default: FIRS (the first available beam or load case if none is specified)

2. X  
   • Description: “Beam abscissa for area stresses from program AQB.”  
     – Defines the longitudinal coordinate along the beam where sectional (area) stresses are reported.  
     – Equivalent in function to NO for case numbering; i.e. you supply an integer or index literal.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (unitless literal coordinate)  
   • Default: FIRS (the first section along the beam, unless overridden)

3. CUTP  
   • Description: “Cut position”  
     – Controls from which side the cut‐section is taken when plotting or listing sectional forces and stresses.  
     – Supported keywords:  
       · LEFT  – cut is taken from the left side of the section  
       · RIGH  – cut is taken from the right side  
       · NONE  – no explicit side; the default behavior  
   • Unit: –/LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: NONE

4. SECT  
   • Description: “Cross‐section number for representations on cross sections (record QUER).”  
     – Selects which cross section to display or list when querying sectional results independent of the beam’s longitudinal coordinate.  
     – Functions like NO for load‐case or design‐case selection.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (integer literal)  
   • Default: FIRS

5. TITL  
   • Description: “Title of the load case in the legend (default as in the database).”  
     – Overrides or supplements the legend entry for the selected load case.  
     – Accepts a text string up to 24 characters (LIT24).  
   • Unit: LIT24 (up to 24 characters literal)  
   • Default: *  (asterisk indicates “use the built‐in title”)

6. HIST  
   • Description: “History case selection”  
     – Picks which load‐ or history‐case trace to draw when showing time‐ or sequence‐dependent results.  
     – Except for NAME/FIND modes, HIST is simply another alias for NO.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (literal integer)  
   • Default: FIRS

Contextual Notes  
• “LC” or “NODE” records control load‐case definitions; “BEAM” and “QUAD” define element types but do not appear in this table.  
• Unused items in this table (T, MAT, REF, NMAT, CS) carry no effect here.  
• When you specify a design load case (for reinforcement or stresses from BEMESS/AQB), all outputs that are stored case‐wise will refer to that design case. Non‐design results still use NO unless you explicitly map them to ENO/X/SECT.  
• Multiple cases or sections can be batched in one listing by providing comma‐ or range‐separated integers. Example:  
     LC NO 1,2,3,4,5  
     LC NO (1 5 1)  
  These forms instruct the system to generate outputs for cases 1 through 5 in sequence.

sections: 3.10 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
See also: NODE, BEAM, QUAD
 LC
 The items T, MAT, REF, NMAT and CS are not used yet.
 The input of a load case or a design load case has an effect at the representation of all results which are stored in reference to the load case.
 Reinforcements, design stresses from the program BEMESS and beam stresses from the pro- gram AQB are represented with the input of the design load case. All other load case-wisely stored results are addressed by NO.
 Results, e.g. stresses, are stored in beam sections. With the input of ENO and X the beam section of current load case is selected.
 It is possible to output more than one load/design/history case or cross section in one list (REPR DLST). For this purpose the numbers have to be written in a row. For example the load cases 1 up to 5 are used in the same list:
 LC NO 1,2,3,4,5
 Or with a generation instruction:
 LC NO (1 5 1)

This table defines the DBO‐record structure used by the ASE/AQB table‐printing programs in SOfiSTiK.  Each row of the table is one “item” (field) in the DBO record; columns give: the item name, a brief description of what it controls, the data type (all are literal strings “LIT” or “–” for numeric values), and the default setting.  When you run a command such as  
  DBO ‘n_disp.pz’ ND 4  
you are creating a DBO record named “n_disp.pz” and setting the ND (decimal places) item to 4.  Likewise, you can change default column widths globally with:  
  DBO ‘*’ WIDT 15  

Item breakdown:  
1. NAME  
  – “Name of the result”  
  – Type: LIT  
  – Default: “!”  
  – Associates a column with a specific result variable in the SOfiSTiK CDBASE.CHM database.  

2. OPTI  
  – Visibility of the column  
  – OFF = not printed; ON = printed  
  – Type: LIT; Default: ON  

3. UNIT  
  – Physical unit/dimension (e.g. m, kN, sec)  
  – Must match a valid UNIT in CDBASE.CHM  
  – Type: LIT; Default: “–”  

4. ND  
  – Number of decimal places in floating-point output  
  – 1–9 = fixed decimal places; E1–E9 = exponential notation with given decimals  
  – Type: LIT; Default: “–”  

5. POS  
  – Column position in the output table or list  
  – Integer column index; if omitted, all columns follow the standard row‐order (load case → locating parameters → results)  
  – Type: numeric; Default: “*” (no change)  

6. WIDT  
  – Width of the column in digits  
  – Type: numeric; Default “*” (inherit previous or global default)  

7. SORT  
  – Sorting mode for this column  
  – NO = no sort; ASCE = ascending; DESC = descending  
  – Type: LIT; Default: NO  

8. REPE  
  – Repetition of recurring values in successive rows  
  – NO = suppress; YES = repeat on every row  
  – Type: LIT; Default: “*” (use global REPE setting)  

9. FORM  
  – Conditional (cell) formatting specification  
  – NO = no formatting; otherwise a two-letter code: format letter + rule letter  
    • Format letters:  
      C = color scale (± from middle)  
      R = color scale (± from edges)  
      W = whole-column coloring  
    • Rule letters:  
      A = apply to all; G = greater than BMAX; S = less than BMIN; B = between BMIN/BMAX; O = outside BMIN/BMAX; E = equal BMIN  
  – Type: LIT; Default: NO  

10. BMIN / BMAX  
  – Lower and upper threshold values for conditional formatting  
  – Units must be in m, kN, or sec to match physical dimensions  
  – Type: numeric; Default: “*” (no limit)  

11. TITL  
  – Override the column’s displayed header text  
  – Type: LIT; Default: “–” (use internal NAME or UNIT label)  

Usage notes and context:  
• Row ordering is by default: load case (or design/cross-section), then localizing values (e.g. beam number, abscissa), and finally the result values.  You can shift a column’s position with POS (e.g. POS 2 moves it to be the second column).  
• By default, repeating values like load case numbers are printed once per page; setting REPE YES forces them to print every row.  
• Floating-point (ND) columns always print their value in every row.  Values of non‐floating columns to the right of a floating column also print every row, regardless of REPE.  
• Conditional formatting (FORM+BMIN+BMAX) works only in the table output, not the internal “Result Browser.”  

This DBO structure gives you full control over which columns appear, how they’re labeled, sorted, sized, repeated, and even color‐coded—enabling highly customized tabular reports directly from the analysis database.

DBO

 All results may be printed in tables, like programs ASE or AQB do. The output options for the tables are set with this record.
 The values of the items NAME and UNIT have to correspond to valid values from the SOfiSTiK database description CDBASE.CHM. The changing of the decimal precision of the nodes sup- port force PZ can be achieved therefore with the following input:

 The items UNIT and ND are also used for graphical results.
 The default of rows order is: First the load case, design case or cross section number, second the values for localizing, e.g. beam number and abscissa, and at last the results values. With the item POSI and a row position input (e.g. 2) the rows order may be changed.
 For clarity reasons the numbers (e.g. load case) will be written once per page if they do not change. It is possible to change this default with the item REPE. Floating-point values are always written in each row.
 Independent from settings using the item REPE, the values of columns which are to the right of a floating point column are always written in each row.
 A conditional formatting, the colouring of table cells, is available with an input to item FORM. The items BMIN and BMAX are limits of the conditional formatting. This formatting is not available for the Result Browser. The literal for the item FORM kann be a combination of one letter for the format and/or one letter for the rule:
