The table shown is the definition of the DIAG record in a data specification. DIAG is a configuration record through which various visual and labeling properties of a diagram can be set. Each row of the table corresponds to one configurable item, together with its description, the unit of measurement or data type, and a default value when the user does not explicitly supply one. Below is a verbal overview of each field, its purpose, valid settings, and default.

1. X  
   • Description: Specifies which dataset or parameter is to be plotted along the horizontal (X) axis of the diagram.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal text)  
   • Default: none (this must normally be supplied by the user)

2. Y  
   • Description: Specifies which dataset or parameter is to be plotted along the vertical (Y) axis.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: none

3. GDEF  
   • Description: A graph‐definition column. This is used to group or differentiate multiple series in a single diagram—for example, different load cases or curve sets.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: none

4. LCTP (Load Case Type Labels)  
   • Description: Controls the text labels shown along the load‐case axis or in legends. You choose one of three modes:  
     – NR: show only the numeric load‐case identifier (number)  
     – NAME: show only the textual description of the load case  
     – NRNM: show both number and name together  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NR

5. YUP (Invert Y Axis)  
   • Description: Determines whether the Y axis should be displayed in its normal orientation (increasing upward) or inverted (increasing downward).  
     – NO: do not invert (standard orientation)  
     – YES: invert the axis  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO

6. LEGE (Legend Display)  
   • Description: Controls the placement of the legend in relation to the diagram.  
     – NO: omit the legend entirely  
     – DIAG: place the legend below the diagram  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: DIAG

7. SPPL (Show Support Placements)  
   • Description: Enables or disables the drawing of support locations (for example boundary or reaction supports) along the axis in structural diagrams.  
     – NO: do not show support placements  
     – YES: render support icons or markers  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO

8. AXFU (Axis Full‐Length Visualization)  
   • Description: Decides whether to extend each axis fully from its minimum to maximum domain limits, even if no data points occupy the entire range.  
     – NO: show axes only over the span of the plotted data  
     – YES: draw axes from absolute min to absolute max  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO

Summary  
The DIAG record consolidates all essential toggles and labels for customizing diagrams in a consistent, scriptable way. Every setting is expressed as a literal (LIT) token. Most parameters have sensible defaults (e.g., no legend omitted, Y axis not inverted), but key inputs (X, Y, GDEF) must generally be specified by the user. This structure makes it straightforward to spin up standard diagrams while retaining the ability to tailor labels, legend placement, axis orientation, and supplementary markings like supports.

DIAG
 Properties of diagrams can be controlled with this record.

The table under consideration defines the input items, their meanings, units and default settings for the DGRA (“diagram graph”) command in the context of an FEM post-processing environment. It serves as a concise reference for how to populate the DGRA record when generating XY-graphs for nodal or element results.

1. General Layout  
 • Four columns:  
  – Item: the keyword used on the DGRA command line.  
  – Description: a brief human-readable label of what that keyword controls.  
  – Unit: the data type or physical unit expected for that item.  
  – Default: the value assumed if the item is omitted.  

2. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
 1. DESC  
  – Item: “DESC”  
  – Description: “Description” – a literal text string that can be used to tag or annotate the resulting graph.  
  – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
  – Default: “–” (no description text applied unless provided)  

 2. VAL1 through VAL5  
  These five rows (VAL1, VAL2, VAL3, VAL4, VAL5) allow the user to specify numerical or enumerated parameters in an ordered list. In practice, VAL1 and VAL2 are the only ones used by DGRA, but the template reserves slots for up to five values if future extensions or variant definitions require more.  
  – VAL1  
   • Description: “Value 1” – typically used to encode the first selection criterion, such as node number or element number.  
   • Unit: “!” indicates a required numeric parameter; its interpretation depends on the surrounding context (node ID, beam ID, etc.).  
   • Default: “–” (no default; must be supplied if VAL1 is referenced)  
  – VAL2, VAL3, VAL4, VAL5  
   • Each carries the label “Value 2,” “Value 3,” etc., indicating placeholder spots.  
   • Unit for each: “–” (not used by standard DGRA definitions unless custom scripting extends the command).  
   • Defaults: all “–”  

 3. AXFL  
  – Item: “AXFL”  
  – Description: “Apply set graph filling color to” – this flag controls whether the area beneath a plotted curve is filled with a background color.  
  – Unit: LIT (literal flag)  
  – Default: X (fill is on by default)  
   • Sub-lines under AXFL explain that “X” applies to the X-axis fill, and “Y” would apply to the Y-axis fill if a second flag position were used.  

3. Usage in Context  
 • In a typical DGRA command, VAL1 and VAL2 specify the defining values for the graph trace. For example, “DGRA VAL1 1020” or “DGRA VAL1 1 VAL2 2.700000” pair with DIAG definitions of X and Y to produce nodal-displacement or beam-force curves.  
 • DESC is optional but recommended for readability and automated reporting, as it stamps the resulting diagram with a descriptive label.  
 • AXFL=X (the default) ensures that the plotted curve is rendered as a filled area under the curve in the diagram. Omitting or overriding AXFL would yield an unfilled line plot.

This structured table enables consistent automated parsing by a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline or vector-store indexing system, ensuring that each DGRA record’s parameters can be reliably extracted, validated, and used to generate engineering graphs without ambiguity.

DGRA
 Graphs can be added to a diagram using this record.
 The following input creates a diagram with the loadcase number on the X axis and the nodal displacement on the Y axis. Graphs will be created for the node numbers 1020 and 1021.
 DIAG X "n_disp.__kwl" Y "n_disp.uz" GDEF "n_disp.nr" DGRA VAL1 1020 DGRA VAL1 1021 NODE TYPE UZ REPR DIAG
 DGRA VAL1 1020
 The following input creates a diagram with the loadcase number on the X axis and the normal force on the Y axis. Graphs will be created for the value pairs beam number = 1 + X = 0.000 and beam number = 1 + X = 2.700.
 DIAG X "beam_for.__kwl" Y "beam_for.n" GDEF "beam_for.nr,beam_for.x" DGRA VAL1 1 VAL2 0 DGRA VAL1 1 VAL2 2.700000 BEAM TYPE N STYP BEAM REPR DIAG

The table shown under the “DIAX” heading defines a small record structure for configuring the properties of a diagram’s axes.  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and four primary entries (AXIS, MODE, TICK, LABL).  Each entry corresponds to a parameter that can be set by the user or taken from built-in defaults.  Below is a detailed breakdown of how to interpret and apply each field:

1. Record Purpose  
   • Name: DIAX  
   • Function: Controls which axis (X or Y) is being modified, how tick marks and labels are generated, and at what spacing.  
   • Context: Used when building or customizing chart or graph frames in a larger plotting or diagramming system.

2. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – The identifier for the property.  This will appear in input or script commands.  
   • Description  
     – A brief, plain-language explanation of what the property does or what values it may accept.  
     – In the case of composite entries (like AXIS), sub-items are indented to clarify the possible choices.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates whether the property’s value is literal (LIT), numeric, or has no units (–).  
     – “LIT” means the value is taken as a literal string or keyword.  
     – A dash (–) means there is no unit designation.  
   • Default  
     – Provides the value assumed if the user does not explicitly set this property.  
     – An exclamation mark (!) indicates that the value must be supplied by the user before the record can take effect.

3. Entries Explained

  • AXIS  
    – Purpose: Specifies which axis of the diagram the subsequent settings will apply to.  
    – Sub-items:  
       • X: Refers to the horizontal axis.  
       • Y: Refers to the vertical axis.  
    – Unit: LIT (expects the literal character “X” or “Y”).  
    – Default: X (if the user does not specify, the record assumes settings apply to the X-axis).

  • MODE  
    – Purpose: Determines how tick marks and label positions are calculated.  
    – Values:  
       • AUTO: The system automatically spaces ticks and labels based on data range and available room.  
       • USER: The user explicitly supplies the spacing intervals.  
    – Unit: LIT (expects the literal keyword “AUTO” or “USER”).  
    – Default: AUTO (automatic generation).

  • TICK  
    – Purpose: When MODE is USER, this defines the numeric interval between successive tick marks along the selected axis.  
    – Unit: – (no unit specifier; simply a numeric spacing value).  
    – Default: ! (mandatory—must be defined by the user in USER mode).

  • LABL  
    – Purpose: When MODE is USER, this sets the numeric interval between labeled tick marks.  These are a subset of the full set of tick marks.  
    – Unit: – (numeric spacing).  
    – Default: ! (mandatory in USER mode).

4. Usage Notes  
   • To adjust only the Y axis with custom spacing, you would set AXIS = Y, MODE = USER, and then supply both TICK and LABL values.  
   • Under AUTO mode, TICK and LABL are ignored; the plotting engine decides optimal spacing.  
   • The default AXIS = X and MODE = AUTO ensures that, without extra input, horizontal axis ticks and labels are automatically placed.

By parsing this table into a vector store, one can quickly retrieve details about each axis parameter—its purpose, valid values, and defaults—enabling dynamic query-driven chart generation or on-the-fly documentation lookup.

DIAX
 Properties of diagram axescan be modified using this record.

The table you’ve provided defines three key properties of the DIAP (Additional Diagram Properties) record.  DIAP is used in conjunction with DLIN (Additional Lines in Diagrams) to control how extra lines are rendered, labeled, and described.  Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and row, including hints as to how you might interpret and store this information in a vector‐based retrieval system (RAG).

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: a short mnemonic code for the property.  
     – Description: human‐readable explanation of the property’s semantics.  
     – Unit: the data type or category of allowed values (for example, LIT stands for literal text).  
     – Default: the value assumed when the property is omitted.  
   • Rows  
     – ALIG  
     – VAL  
     – DESC

2. Row‐by‐row Detail

  • ALIG (Alignment of the line)  
    – Description: Specifies how the added line is oriented relative to a reference point or baseline in the diagram.  
    – Allowed Values:  
      • HOR — horizontal alignment  
      • VER — vertical alignment  
    – Unit: LIT (literal string). This indicates you store it as text, not numeric or Boolean.  
    – Default: HOR. If no alignment is explicitly defined, the line will be drawn horizontally.  

  • VAL (Value)  
    – Description: Represents the numeric or textual “value” associated with the extra line.  In many diagramming contexts this might be a measure, a label number, a scale factor, or some domain‐specific code.  
    – Unit: – (none specified). This means VAL can be interpreted according to context; no rigid data‐type annotation is enforced.  
    – Default: “!” (an exclamation mark). In some systems an exclamation mark flags a required field or a placeholder for user input.  

  • DESC (Description)  
    – Description: A free‐form text field where the user can provide a descriptive annotation for the line.  This might explain its purpose, parameterize it in natural language, or comment on its role in the larger diagram.  
    – Unit: LIT (literal). This is unstructured text, so you can store complete sentences, phrases, or even bulleted notes.  
    – Default: “–” (a hyphen). A hyphen typically indicates “no description provided.”  

3. Contextual Usage in RAG Vector Store  
   When ingesting DIAP records into your vector store, you can treat each property as a separate field or embed them together in a single JSON/text blob.  A recommended approach:  
   • Create a document per DIAP record, with fields “alignment,” “value,” and “description.”  
   • Include the default fallback values explicitly, so that downstream consumers know what happens when a property isn’t set.  
   • Index the “Description” field for semantic search to catch queries like “horizontal annotation” or “add vertical label.”  
   • Store “ALIG” and “VAL” as metadata tags or filter attributes for efficient faceted search (e.g., find all lines set to VER alignment).  

4. Example JSON Representation  
  {  
    "property": "DIAP",  
    "alignment": { "value": "HOR", "type": "LIT", "default": "HOR" },  
    "value": { "value": "!", "type": "None", "default": "!" },  
    "description": { "value": "-", "type": "LIT", "default": "-" }  
  }  

5. Summary  
   This table defines the minimal but essential controls for positioning (ALIG), labeling (VAL), and annotating (DESC) supplemental lines in technical diagrams.  By capturing these fields in your RAG pipeline—complete with units and defaults—you ensure accurate retrieval, clear fallbacks, and seamless integration with any client that generates or interprets diagrammatic data.

The excerpt you’ve provided is taken from “3.16 DIAP – Additional diagram properties” and documents two configurable parameters that apply when generating or annotating diagrams via the DIAP record. In many diagram-generation systems (particularly those conforming to a vector-store or RAG environment), you first use the DLIN record to insert extra drawing lines; immediately thereafter, DIAP lets you fine-tune how those lines are labeled and how text is rendered. Below is a breakdown of the table’s structure and each field in context.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: The mnemonic or keyword used in the DIAP record.  
     – Description: A human-readable explanation of what the parameter controls.  
     – Unit: The unit of measurement or type for the parameter value.  
     – Default: The value assumed if you do not explicitly specify the parameter.  
   • Rows  
     – Each row corresponds to one parameter. In this snippet, two parameters appear: SCHH and TXT.

2. Parameters Detailed  

  A. SCHH  
   • Item name: SCHH  
   • Description: “Text height”  
     – Controls the size of any text labels that accompany your additional lines or diagram elements.  
     – Affects all text rendered after this setting takes effect, until overridden.  
   • Unit: “—” (unitless)  
     – You supply a pure numeric scale factor. No physical dimension (inches, mm) is implied; it’s relative to the diagram’s internal coordinate system.  
   • Default: 0.2  
     – If you omit SCHH in your DIAP record, the system will render text at 20% of the default stroke height or baseline font size.

  B. TXT  
   • Item name: TXT  
   • Description: “Print used pairs of values as table”  
     – Enables or disables automatic generation of a small tabular legend that lists every pair of coordinate or parameter values you’ve “used” in DLIN or related records.  
     – If you draw multiple patterned lines or data series, the legend helps viewers correlate line style with numeric parameters.  
   • Unit: LIT  
     – Denotes a literal enumeration rather than a numeric measurement.  
     – Acceptable literals (case-insensitive):  
       • YES: Instructs the system to output the table of used value-pairs immediately following the diagram.  
       • NO: Suppresses that table entirely.  
   • Default: NO  
     – By default, no legend table is printed. You must explicitly set “TXT=YES” if you want the tabulated output.

3. How to Use in a DIAP Record  
   • A typical DIAP invocation might look like:  
     DIAP SCHH=0.3 TXT=YES  
   • This would enlarge all labels to 30% of base size and append a value-pair legend.  
   • If you only want to adjust text height, you could write:  
     DIAP SCHH=0.15  
   • Conversely, to leave height at 0.2 but show a legend:  
     DIAP TXT=YES

4. Relationship to DLIN  
   • The DLIN record governs the drawing of extra lines—specifying endpoints, colors, dash patterns, etc.  
   • DIAP refines how those lines are annotated, ensuring that text labels appear at a consistent size and that a summary legend can be auto-generated.

By indexing these parameters in a vector store, you can rapidly retrieve not only the mnemonic (SCHH, TXT) but also the full description, type, and default behavior whenever a user queries “diagram text size” or “enable legend table.” This improves both the fidelity of generated diagrams and the clarity of user-facing documentation.

DLIN
 Additional lines in diagrams can be added using this record.
 3.16 DIAP – Additional diagram properties
 DIAP

The table below defines the two input items for the “DLAB” (display‐label) record, which controls how and which result values get textual labels when you post‐process or plot your SoFiSTiK output. In a typical workflow you first use FLT (filter) or FILT (extreme‐value selection) to reduce your result set, and then you invoke DLAB to selectively label numeric values on a graphic.  

Table structure  
• Item  
  – The keyword of the input parameter.  
• Description  
  – A brief explanation of what the parameter does and, where applicable, the list of permitted literal settings along with their meanings.  
• Unit  
  – The kind of value expected: “LIT” indicates a literal string token; a dash (–) means a numeric or unitless quantity.  
• Default  
  – The value assumed when the parameter is omitted.  

| Item  | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                | Unit | Default |
|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------|---------|
| MODE  | Values to be labeled. Choose one of the following literal options:  
         • NONE  – no labels are placed on the results.  
         • GLEX  – only the single most extreme (global max and min) value in the entire result set.  
         • EXTR  – all local extreme values (peaks and valleys) are labeled.  
         • ALL   – every value in the result set receives a label.  
         • E2ND  – label every 2nd value.  
         • E3RD  – label every 3rd value.  
         • E4TH  – label every 4th value.  
         • E5TH  – label every 5th value.                                                                                                                          | LIT  | NONE    |
| THRH  | Threshold value between extreme values to be labeled (applies only when MODE = EXTR).  
         • A nonzero positive number here suppresses the labeling of minor local extrema whose difference from a neighboring extremum falls below this threshold.  
         • Use THRH = 0 to label every local extremum regardless of magnitude.                                                       | –    | 0       |

Detailed notes on each parameter  

1. MODE  
   – Controls the density and type of labels attached to your post‐processed result (for example, nodal displacements, internal forces, stresses, etc.).  
   – “LIT” unit code indicates you must spell the option exactly as shown (case‐sensitive).  
   – Default NONE leaves your output clean (no labels). Change to GLEX or EXTR for extremal values, ALL for full coverage, or Enth for periodic sampling.  

2. THRH  
   – A purely numeric, dimensionless cutoff used only in conjunction with MODE=EXTR.  
   – If you set THRH > 0, any local peak or valley whose difference from its adjacent value is smaller than THRH will not be labeled. This helps avoid clutter from trivial fluctuations.  
   – When omitted, THRH defaults to 0, meaning every local extremum—no matter how slight—is annotated.  

Example usage  
– To label only the global maximum and minimum displacement values in a result table:  
     DLAB MODE GLEX  
– To mark all local peaks and valleys that exceed a vertical difference of 0.05 units:  
     DLAB MODE EXTR THRH 0.05  
– To place labels on every 4th value along each result curve:  
     DLAB MODE E4TH  

By properly selecting MODE (and, where needed, THRH), you can tailor your graphics or tabular outputs to highlight just the information you need, keeping your plots readable and your data presentations focused.

The table shown defines the schema of the FLT record, which is used to assemble and control filter criteria when querying SOFiSTiK result tables. Each row in a FLT record describes one single filter clause; multiple clauses sharing the same ID form an AND-group, while clauses with different IDs are OR-joined. Here is a breakdown of each field (column) in that table:

1. ID  
   – Description: Identifies a filter set. All filters bearing the same ID number are AND–combined; different IDs become OR–combined.  
   – Unit: “—” (no unit)  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory; user must supply a positive integer > 0)  
   – Constraints:  
     • Must be an integer greater than zero.  
     • All filters belonging to the same logical group share an identical ID.  

2. NAME  
   – Description: The exact name of the result quantity to be filtered. Typical examples are nodal or element result codes such as “n_disp.nr” (node number) or “n_disp.ux” (nodal displacement in X).  
   – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory; user must supply a valid result name)  
   – Constraints:  
     • Must match one of the entries in the SOFiSTiK database description (CDBASE.CHM).  
     • Case and spelling must exactly correspond to the database registry.  

3. RULE  
   – Description: The filter condition—an expression that evaluates the value of the field given by NAME. Examples include “>1009”, “=1010”, “<0.1”, or compound expressions if supported.  
   – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   – Default: “!” (mandatory; user must supply a valid comparison or match expression)  
   – Constraints:  
     • Follows the syntax rules for numeric or string comparison as defined by SOFiSTiK.  
     • Operators such as >, <, =, BETWEEN, etc., must be used in a manner consistent with the data type of the result.  

4. ACT  
   – Description: Controls the visibility or activation state of the filter.  
       • YES → filter is active (default)  
       • NO  → filter is deactivated or hidden  
   – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   – Default: YES  
   – Behavior:  
       • If set to NO, the filter clause exists in the record but is ignored at query time.  
       • Setting ACT to YES re-enables the clause without needing to retype NAME or RULE.  

Usage Patterns (context):  
• Defining an AND group:  
    FLT ID 1 NAME “n_disp.nr” RULE “>1009”  
    FLT ID 1 NAME “n_disp.ux” RULE “>0.1”  
  → This filters for all rows where node number > 1009 AND X-displacement > 0.1.  
• Defining an OR group:  
    FLT ID 1 NAME “n_disp.nr” RULE “1010”  
    FLT ID 2 NAME “n_disp.nr” RULE “1020”  
  → This yields rows where node number equals 1010 OR equals 1020.  

By capturing the items ID, NAME, RULE, and ACT in a standardized table, the FLT record provides a flexible, declarative mechanism to compose complex filter logic—combining multiple criteria with AND/OR semantics—directly in SOFiSTiK’s result‐extraction layer.

Below is a self-contained, detailed description of the filter-syntax table you provided.  It explains each operator’s purpose, its semantics, and gives examples.  This description can be embedded alongside your FLT/FILT documentation in a RAG-powered vector store to help users construct valid RULE strings.

1.  Negation  
    •  Syntax: “!”  
    •  Semantics: Negates the entire following expression.  
    •  Example: RULE "!>100" returns all values not greater than 100 (i.e. ≤100).

2.  Equality  
    •  Syntax: “X” or “=X”  
    •  Semantics: Matches values exactly equal to X.  Both forms are interchangeable.  
    •  Examples:  
       –  RULE "5"  → selects entries whose field equals 5.  
       –  RULE "=OK" → selects entries whose field equals the text “OK”.

3.  Inequalities  
    •  Syntax & Meaning:  
       –  “>X” : values strictly greater than X  
       –  “>=X”: values greater than or equal to X  
       –  “<X” : values strictly less than X  
       –  “<=X”: values less than or equal to X  
    •  Examples:  
       –  RULE ">0.1" filters out all results whose numeric value is ≤0.1.  
       –  RULE "<=1009" ensures node numbers do not exceed 1009.

4.  Closed and Open Numeric Ranges  
    You can specify intervals with semicolon separators.  Brackets control inclusion/exclusion at each end.  
    •  “[FROM;TO]”   : FROM ≤ value ≤ TO  
    •  “[FROM;TO[”   : FROM ≤ value < TO  
    •  “]FROM;TO]”   : FROM < value ≤ TO  
    •  “]FROM;TO[”   : FROM < value < TO  
    •  Syntax for incremental steps: “(FROM;TO;INCR)”  
         –  Semantics: enumerates values between FROM and TO, stepping by INCR.  
         –  Example: RULE “(0;1;0.1)” matches 0.0, 0.1, 0.2, …, up to 1.0.  

5.  Wildcard Text Matching  
    •  Asterisk (*)  
       –  Matches any sequence of characters (including none).  
       –  Example: RULE "max*" selects all text values beginning with “max”, such as “maxDisp”, “maximum”.  
    •  Question mark (?)  
       –  Matches exactly one character.  
       –  Example: RULE "a?c" matches “abc” or “a1c” but not “abbc” or “ac”.

How These Rules Plug into FLT and FILT  
–  In your FLT records, you assign a RULE string exactly as shown above.  
–  Multiple FLT lines sharing the same ID form an AND-set: all conditions must be true.  
–  Different IDs are OR-joined: any one set of conditions suffices.  
–  FILT (extreme-value selection) also understands these RULE syntaxes when you add or remove filters by TYPE.  

By storing this description alongside your vectorized docs for FLT/FILT, users receive immediate, rich guidance on constructing valid RULE expressions for filtering SOFiSTiK results.

The table shown defines the input record “FILT,” which is used in conjunction with the SOFiSTiK database to perform extreme‐value selection on results tables. Each row of the table corresponds to one parameter (or “item”) of the FILT record; columns specify the item name, a brief description of its purpose, the unit of measure, and the default value if the item is omitted. Below is a detailed description of each item and how it is used in practice:

1. NAME  
   • Purpose: Specifies the result quantity to be filtered. Typical examples are nodal displacements (“n_disp.ux”) or element forces (“e_forc.mx”), provided that these names exactly match entries in the SOFiSTiK database definition file (CDBASE.CHM).  
   • Unit: LIT (literal string) – The user must supply the identifier exactly as it appears in the database.  
   • Default: “!” – A mandatory field. If omitted, the record is considered invalid.

2. TYPE  
   • Purpose: Determines whether to perform no filtering (i.e. pass through all values) or to extract extreme values only.  
   • Allowed Values:  
     – NO: No filtering applied; all values are shown.  
     – EX: Extreme‐value filtering; only minima, maxima, or both are retained, depending on the EXTP setting.  
   • Unit: LIT – A literal code word, either NO or EX.  
   • Default: “!” – Must be provided; no default “fallback” is permitted.

3. EXRF  
   • Purpose: Reference column(s) used when grouping results for extreme‐value selection. When TYPE is set to EX, you can specify one or more columns by name; the FILT logic then computes extreme values separately for each unique combination of those reference columns. For example, you might specify “LOADCASE” so that each load case yields its own min/max set.  
   • Unit: LIT – A comma‐separated list of valid database column names, matching CDBASE.CHM entries.  
   • Default: “–” (dash) – If left blank while TYPE=EX, FILT will compute extreme values over the entire result set without grouping.

4. EXTP  
   • Purpose: Indicates which extreme values to select when TYPE=EX.  
   • Allowed Values:  
     – MIN: Only the minimum value in each reference group (or overall if no EXRF) is kept.  
     – MAX: Only the maximum value in each group.  
     – MIMA: Both minimum and maximum values are kept (this is the default behavior if EXTP is omitted).  
   • Unit: LIT – Literal keywords MIN, MAX, or MIMA.  
   • Default: MIMA – If the user fails to supply EXTP, the record will default to extracting both minima and maxima.

Usage Example:  
To extract minimum and maximum nodal displacements in the X‐direction (“n_disp.ux”) for each load case defined in column “LC_NO,” one would write:  
FILT NAME “n_disp.ux” TYPE EX EXRF “LC_NO” EXTP MIMA  

In summary, the FILT record provides a concise mechanism to request global or grouped extreme‐value filtering on any tabulated result recognized by the SOFiSTiK database. The four items—NAME, TYPE, EXRF, and EXTP—collectively control which result is examined, how it is filtered, how groups (if any) are defined, and whether minima, maxima, or both are returned.

This table is a parameter‐definition specification for the JOIN command in a data‐processing context. It lists exactly two items—COL1 and COL2—that the JOIN function requires to merge two result tables. Each row describes one required parameter; each column in the table defines a particular aspect of those parameters.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns:  
     – Item: The internal parameter name used in the JOIN command.  
     – Description: A short human‐readable explanation of what the parameter represents.  
     – Unit: The data type or format accepted for the parameter (“LIT” indicates a literal string).  
     – Default: The value assumed if no explicit value is given (“!” denotes that no default exists, making the parameter mandatory).  

   • Rows:  
     – COL1: Refers to the column name in the first table to be used as the join key.  
     – COL2: Refers to the column name in the second table to be used as the join key.  

2. Semantics of Each Column  
   – Item  
     • Purpose: Identifies the parameter’s programmatic name.  
     • Domain: Two fixed identifiers—COL1 and COL2.  
     • Usage: Users issue “COL1 <column_name>” and “COL2 <column_name>” to specify which columns in each table to align.  

   – Description  
     • Purpose: Clarifies that both COL1 and COL2 refer to “Name of the column.”  
     • Context: Guides the user that the values supplied must match existing column headers in the respective result tables.  

   – Unit  
     • Declares that acceptable input must be of type literal string (“LIT”).  
     • Implies no numeric, boolean, or complex structure is permitted—only plain text that exactly matches a column label.  

   – Default  
     • “!” signals there is no built‐in default; the parameter is required.  
     • The JOIN operation will fail or prompt an error if either COL1 or COL2 is not explicitly provided.  

3. Usage in the JOIN Workflow  
   • Prerequisite: Two separate query results, each having a single parameter column with matching values (e.g. “LC” for loadcases).  
   • Execution: By supplying COL1 and COL2, the engine knows which column from result set A should pair with which column from result set B.  
   • Outcome: A unified table where rows from both inputs are combined along the specified keys, bringing together all other columns side by side.  

4. Relationship to Broader Export/Reporting  
   • This parameter table is part of a larger command sequence that can produce on‐screen tables, diagrams, or exports (XLSX/CSV).  
   • Downstream records (e.g., node coordinates, displacements) will appear in the merged table under newly joined headings.  

5. Constraints and Validation  
   • Both COL1 and COL2 must be nonempty strings matching existing column names.  
   • No duplicates: If the same column name is used for COL1 and COL2, the join may yield a trivial self‐join.  
   • Error handling: Missing or misspelled column names will trigger export failures or runtime errors.  

In summary, this concise two‐row table strictly defines the two mandatory text parameters (COL1 and COL2) that drive how the JOIN command aligns columns across separate result sets. Each parameter is a literal string without a default, ensuring explicit user control over the key fields used in data merging.

The screenshot shows the definition of the input‐record parameters for an “XLSX – Excel Export” (or CSV export) in a result‐viewer or data‐reporting module.  Each row in the table describes one configurable field of the export command, giving:

• Item – the keyword used on the command line or in a script  
• Description – a brief explanation of what the field controls  
• Unit – the type of the field (here all are literal, LIT, or simple integers)  
• Default – the default value used if the user does not supply an override  

Below is a detailed breakdown of each parameter:

1. NAME  
   – File name  
   – Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   – Default: “!” (typically forces an interactive prompt for the name)  

2. WS  
   – Worksheet name (only relevant when TYPE = XLSX)  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: “XLSX‐Export”  

3. ROW  
   – Starting row index in the worksheet (only when TYPE = XLSX)  
   – Unit: integer  
   – Default: 1  

4. COL  
   – Starting column index in the worksheet (only when TYPE = XLSX)  
   – Unit: integer  
   – Default: 1  

5. CLNM  
   – Export column titles  
     • NO: do not write header row  
     • YES: include header row  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: YES  

6. TIME  
   – Export the current date and time into the output  
     • NO: skip timestamp  
     • YES: include timestamp  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: NO  

7. CDB  
   – Export the name of the selected database  
     • NO: skip database name  
     • YES: include database name  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: NO  

8. ELEM  
   – Export information on loadcase and element selection  
     • NO: skip loadcase/element metadata  
     • YES: include that metadata  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: NO  

9. FILT  
   – Export filter information applied to the data  
     • NO: skip filter settings  
     • YES: include filter details  
   – Unit: LIT  
   – Default: NO  

10. RESU  
    – Export the table’s title  
      • NO: do not export title  
      • YES: export title line  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: NO  

11. TYPE  
    – Type of the exported file  
      • XLSX: Excel Workbook format  
      • CSV: plain‐text, comma (or other) delimited  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: XLSX  

12. DELI  
    – Delimiter to use when TYPE = CSV  
      • COMM: comma  
      • TAB: tab  
      • COLO: colon  
      • SEMI: semicolon  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: COMM  

Notes and context:

The input table defines the structure and permissible values of a “TINF” record, which controls what summary information is shown at the end of a generated table.  This record is especially relevant in environments that distinguish between interactive result‐viewer sessions and report generation.  By specifying different TINF settings, users can tailor which aggregate rows (minimum, maximum, total, or all) appear, and on which output medium they appear.

Overall Layout  
• Four columns:  
  – Item: the parameter name within the TINF record.  
  – Description: human‐readable explanation plus subcodes.  
  – Unit: always “LIT,” indicating that each parameter takes literal text codes.  
  – Default: the parameter’s assumed value when the TINF record omits it (a dash indicates “no default”).

Parameter Rows  
1. TYPE  
   • Description: “Type of information.”  
     – ALL = All summary rows (minimum, maximum, total) are displayed.  
     – MIN = Only the minimum row is displayed.  
     – MAX = Only the maximum row is displayed.  
     – TOTA = Only the total row is displayed.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: none (user must explicitly choose which summary type if they include a TYPE entry).

2. MEDI  
   • Description: “Affected output.”  
     – INT = User Interface (Result Viewer)  
     – REP = Report  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: INT (if the user omits MEDI, the settings apply to interactive sessions by default).

3. OPTI  
   • Description: “Visibility.”  
     – NO = Not visible  
     – YES = Visible  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: none (visibility must be set explicitly per combination of TYPE and MEDI).

Behavior When No TINF Record Is Provided  
If the system does not find any TINF record in the request, it applies built‐in defaults depending on whether the output is interactive or a printed report:

• Interactive (Result Viewer) defaults:  
  – MIN NO  
  – MAX NO  
  – TOTA NO  
  → No summary rows appear in the live interface.  

• Report defaults:  
  – MIN YES  
  – MAX YES  
  – TOTA NO  
  → When generating a formal report, both the minimum and maximum rows are shown, but totals are suppressed.

The table is a schema for defining “fill‐area” properties in a graphics or rendering system. It consists of four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and is organized into three logical groups of parameters. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. Columns  
- Item: The mnemonic or short code used to specify a particular parameter.  
- Description: A brief human‐readable explanation of what the parameter controls.  
- Unit: The data type or measurement unit of the parameter. In this table “LIT” denotes a literal token or indexed value, and “–” indicates a numeric value without a special unit.  
- Default: The value assumed if the parameter is not explicitly set.

2. Group 1 – Element Selection (ID1 through ID4)  
• ID1, ID2, ID3, ID4  
  • Description: Each of these four IDs represents an “Element” slot in the fill‐area record. A user can populate up to four separate element references to control which graphical entities participate in the fill.  
  • Unit: LIT (literal)—each ID takes a name or index of an element.  
  • Default:  
    – ID1 defaults to “!”. This is likely a special token meaning “all” or “first.”  
    – ID2, ID3, ID4 default to “–” (blank), indicating no secondary elements are selected by default.

3. Group 2 – Color by Predefined Index (COLO)  
• COLO  
  • Description: Selects a fill color from a fixed palette of named indices. Under the Description column you see a sub‐list of all valid tokens and their associated colors:  
    – BLCK → black  
    – RED → red  
    – GREE → green  
    – BLUE → blue  
    – YELL → yellow  
    – MAGE → magenta  
    – CYAN → cyan  
    – BROW → brown  
    – GRAY → gray  
    – WHIT → white  
    – NONE → none (no fill)  
  • Unit: LIT—you specify exactly one of these text tokens.  
  • Default: “–” (none selected).

4. Group 3 – Explicit RGBA Color Values (R, G, B, A)  
• R, G, B, A  
  • Description: Instead of using a named index, you can define the fill color explicitly by specifying red, green, blue, and alpha (opacity) channels.  
    – R: R‐Value of RGB color  
    – G: G‐Value of RGB color  
    – B: B‐Value of RGB color  
    – A: A‐Value (alpha) of RGB color—controls transparency, with 255 being fully opaque.  
  • Unit: “–” (numeric byte, range 0–255).  
  • Default: 255 for each channel, which yields pure white at full opacity if no other color index is set.

Usage notes:  
- You may choose either a color index via COLO or explicit RGBA values; typically a system will prioritize explicit RGBA when provided.  
- Element IDs allow complex fill definitions that span multiple shapes or regions.  
- Default settings ensure a fully opaque white fill of “Element 1” when the record is instantiated with no overrides.

The input table defines three configurable parameters—SHOW, OVLP, and EXTR—each controlling a specific aspect of how results or annotations appear in an output (for example, a plot or report). Every parameter is identified by a short name in the Item column, accompanied by a human-readable Description, the type of values it accepts (Unit), and its built-in default setting.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Item: A three- or four-letter keyword used to invoke the parameter.  
   • Description: A concise explanation of what the parameter does. Sub-lines list the permissible literal (LIT) values and their meanings.  
   • Unit: Indicates that the parameter expects a literal string (LIT) from the enumerated options.  
   • Default: The preselected setting applied when the user does not explicitly override the parameter.

2. Parameter Details  

   A. SHOW (Number of results)  
     – Purpose: Determines which subset of results is displayed.  
     – Allowed values:  
       • ALL: Display every result, regardless of statistical significance or relevance thresholds.  
       • SIGN: Show only those results deemed significant according to predefined criteria.  
     – Unit: LIT (one of the keywords ALL or SIGN)  
     – Default: SIGN  

   B. OVLP (Checking for text overlapping)  
     – Purpose: Controls whether the system checks for overlapping text labels (for example, in a chart) and how it responds if overlaps occur.  
     – Allowed values:  
       • OFF: Disable any checking; text labels may overlap freely.  
       • AMAX: Enable overlap detection and, in cases where labels collide, display only the one with the largest absolute value.  
     – Unit: LIT (OFF or AMAX)  
     – Default: AMAX  

   C. EXTR (Annotation of minimum and maximum value)  
     – Purpose: Specifies whether to annotate the extreme (minimum and maximum) data points in a visualization or output.  
     – Allowed values:  
       • NO: Do not add any annotation for extremes.  
       • YES: Actively mark and label both the minimum and maximum data values.  
     – Unit: LIT (NO or YES)  
     – Default: YES  

3. Usage Context and Notes  
   • These parameters are designed to be combined in a single command line or function call, e.g., “SHOW=ALL OVLP=OFF EXTR=NO.”  
   • Because all Units are literal tokens, the system performs a direct string comparison against the enumerated options.  
   • Defaults ensure a balanced output—significant items only (SHOW=SIGN), overlap‐aware labeling (OVLP=AMAX), and extreme annotations enabled (EXTR=YES). Users can override any or all defaults to tailor the presentation.

The table defines the parameters accepted by the VIEW command for specifying a three-dimensional projection. It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and lists six parameters (rows) that together control the type of projection, the direction or angles of view, the downward-pointing axis, and any additional rotation. Below is a detailed narrative breakdown of each entry.

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Determines how the viewing direction is defined. You must choose one of three modes:  
     – “DIRE” or “STAN” for a parallel projection defined by a direction vector,  
     – “ANGL” for an angular definition of each axis relative to the horizontal.  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Default: “DEFA”  
   • Notes from context:  
     – If TYPE = DIRE or STAN, the viewer is assumed at infinite distance, and X,Y,Z give the components of a vector pointing either behind (DIRE) or in front of (STAN) the scene origin.  
     – If TYPE = ANGL, X, Y, Z are angles (x°, y°, z°) of the X-, Y-, Z-axes relative to the horizontal plane. Care must be taken to avoid degenerate orientations (e.g., two axes perpendicular or parallel to the projection plane), which can yield an ambiguous or undefined view.

2. X, Y, Z  
   • Description: Three numeric inputs whose meaning depends on TYPE.  
     – For DIRE/STAN: real-valued vector components (no explicit unit).  
     – For ANGL: rotational angles in degrees.  
   • Unit: none (–)  
   • Default: 0 for each component

3. AXIS  
   • Description: Specifies which coordinate axis points downwards on the drawing, applicable only when TYPE is DIRE or STAN.  
   • Unit: Literal (LIT)  
   • Default: “*” (automatic or unspecified)  
   • Possible values:  
     – ALTE: rotate the entire view by 180° about the line of sight  
     – POSX, POSY, POSZ: force the positive X-, Y-, or Z-axis to point downward  
     – NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ: force the negative X-, Y-, or Z-axis to point downward

4. ROTA  
   • Description: A further in-plane rotation of the projected view, measured clockwise.  
   • Unit: DEGREE  
   • Default: 0°

By adjusting these six parameters, users can fully control the orientation, perspective, and rotation of the three-dimensional structure rendered on the sheet. The separation between a direction-vector mode (DIRE/STAN) and an angular mode (ANGL) allows flexibility: vector mode is useful for precise parallel projections along a known direction, while angular mode gives direct control over how each axis tilts relative to horizontal. The AXIS setting resolves any ambiguity in the “downward” direction, and ROTA lets you fine-tune the final spin of the image without altering the main viewing vector or angles.

See also:
 VIEW
 The three?dimensional view specification of the representation is described by VIEW. The input defines a parallel projection via the line of vision and orientation of the drawing at the sheet.
 The user has the following possibilities for the representation and orientation of the structure on the picture:
 TYPE = DIRE or STAN
 The values X, Y and Z are components of the direction in which the observer is looking. The observer stands in infinite distance in case of parallel projection. Thus X, Y and Z are coordi- nates of a point which lies from the observer directly behind (DIRE) or in front of (STAN) the origin of the coordinate system. The value of AXIS defines the axis which shows downwards for the observer.
 TYPE = ANGL
 The three inputs for X, Y and Z describe the angles x,y,z of the corresponding axes towards the horizontal direction. The three values can be selected arbitrarily. However, attention has to be paid, that the graphical representation can be degenerate with an input of two orientations standing vertically to each other or parallelly. These degenerations describe either an axis vertical to the optical plane or a non unambiguously defined illustration.

The table shown defines the four keyword-parameters you can use when requesting structural results in a RAG-driven vector store.  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and lists the following parameters:

1.  TYPE  
    •  Kind of structural value to be retrieved (for example forces, moments, displacements, stresses—see “tables below”).  
    •  Unit: LIT (it expects a literal code rather than a number).  
    •  Default: none (you must specify TYPE explicitly).

2.  ETYP  
    •  When TYPE has been chosen, ETYP lets you restrict the request to one or more element-types (beams, shells, springs, tendons, boundaries, etc.).  A full list of supported element types (with their system codes, e.g. BEAM, DSLN, SPRI, BTEN, BOUN…) appears elsewhere in the document.  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: none (you must specify ETYP if you wish to filter by element type).

3.  REPR  
    •  The form—or “representation”—in which you want your results returned.  Allowed literals are:  
       –  DSTR  Structure representation (full geometry)  
       –  DTXT  Text representation (one line per value)  
       –  DVEC  Vector representation (arrows, e.g. for displacements, forces)  
       –  DLIN  Line representation (contour lines)  
       –  DIAG  Diagram representation (graphical plots)  
       –  DLST  Text list (tabular list)  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: “∗” (a program default will be chosen based on the TYPE if you omit REPR).  
    •  Note: if you choose DIAG, you will need to consult the DIAG section for further diagram-specific settings.

4.  FILL  
    •  Defines whether and how colored fills or shaded zones appear in your graphical output.  Allowed literals are:  
       –  NO    No fill—simple solid colors only.  
       –  VARC  No fill, but colors vary per element or group.  
       –  AREA  Fills the area enclosed by the elements with variable colors (contours).  
       –  VERT  For line-based drawings: draw color bars perpendicular to the basic line.  
       –  PARA  For line-based drawings: draw color bars parallel to the basic line.  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: NO  

—  
Additional Context from the Manual  
•  If you do not explicitly set REPR, FILL or ETYP, the software will assign a “program default” based on the TYPE you have selected and on internal rules (see the STRU/TYPE defaults list).  
•  Some TYPE values only make sense with certain ETYPs—these allowable pairings are marked by an asterisk (“∗”) in the master STRU/TYPE table.  
•  Beyond these four parameters, further sub-options (cross-section choices, load-case filters, grouping flags, life-cycle phases, etc.) may be available depending on TYPE and ETYP. Those appear in subsequent tables covering CROS, MAT, LC, MLCT, MLCA, and other legacy keywords.  

In practice, a complete result request might look like:  
   STRU,TYPE=MYPL,ETYP=BEAM,REPR=DVEC,FILL=AREA  
This will return fully-plastic bending moments My (TYPE=MYPL) on beam elements only, rendered as colored vectors that fill the beam cross-section.

The table you’ve provided is essentially a registry of all “named” result quantities that can be produced by a structural‐analysis engine, along with the contexts in which each quantity is defined and the levels at which it can be reported.  Below is a guided tour of its key parts.

1.  Overall Layout  
   - Columns 1–8 define the identity and nature of each result quantity:  
     • Literal: the short code used in the software (e.g. LENG, RFBE)  
     • Meaning: a brief description in plain English (e.g. Length, Contained mass of bending reinforcements)  
     • NAME, TYPE, STRU, NUMN, REPR, FILL: internal classification fields used to select defaults, group results, choose representations or fill options.  
     • ETYP: the element‐or‐entity type to which this result applies (see below).  
     • DIM: the physical dimension and unit (m, t, kNm, mm, etc.).  
   - The remaining nine columns (headed T, E, M, G, R, C, D, N, Q) are flags: each is marked “*” when this quantity is available at that aggregation level:  
     • T = total (global sum)  
     • E = per element  
     • M = per material  
     • G = per group  
     • R = per secondary group  
     • C = per cross section  
     • D = per design‐element member  
     • N = per design secondary group  
     • Q = per design cross section  

2.  Header Notes and Defaults  
   - If REPR (representation), FILL (fill type) or ETYP are not specified explicitly for a given result TYPE, program defaults will be selected.  
   - For diagram‐style outputs, REPR=DIAG and you must consult the separate DIAG specification.  
   - The general STRU TYPE (structure‐type grouping) applies unless an ETYP‐specific literal overrides it; overriding rows are marked with “∗” in the rightmost availability columns.

3.  Entity Types (ETYP)  
   The table is organized in blocks, each block applying to a different ETYP (element or system entity):  
   - ETYP=MAT (Materials): e.g. BT (elastic bedding tangential, kN/m³).  
   - ETYP=CROS (Cross sections): e.g. AK (torsional equivalent area, m²), MYPL/MZPL (fully plastic bending moments, kNm), MBPL (warping moment, kNm²), YSPL/ZSPL (plastic center coordinates, mm), and their “design” equivalents (M2PD, YSPD, ZSPD).  
   - ETYP=BTEN / DTEN (Beam or design‐element tendons) – supports tendon‐related result codes.  
   - ETYP=BOUN (Boundary elements), ETYP=SPRI (Spring elements), ETYP=DSLN (Design elements), ETYP=BEAM (Beam sections), ETYP=LC (Load cases).  
   - Each block begins with a short descriptor (“System Values of the Spring Elements”, etc.) and then lists the “Literal” names and meanings.

4.  Sample Quantities and Dimensions  
   - LENG (Length) / unit m  
   - RFBE (bending reinforcement mass) / t  
   - RFSH (shear reinforcement mass) / t  
   - TEND (tendon mass) / t  

5.  Availability Flags  
   - In the row for, say, LENG, an asterisk under every column T, E, M, G, R, C, D, N, Q means you can request “length” at any of those aggregation levels.  
   - If a star is missing under a given heading, that report level is not supported for that quantity.

6.  Life‐Cycle‐Assessment (LCA) Extension  
   A second adjacent table follows the same pattern for LCA metrics:  
   - MLCT: total LCA impact  
   - MLCA: per phase  
   - MLCM: per material  
   - MLPM: per material‐phase  
   - MLCG: per group  
   - MLPG: per group‐phase  
   - MLCS / MLPS: per secondary group (and per phase)  
   - MLCY / MLPY / MLCD / MLPD: various combinations of structural member vs. secondary group and phase  
   - Availability flags here use slightly different letters (T,P,M,N,G,H,R,S,Y,Z,D,E) but follow exactly the same “star = supported” convention.

In practice, when you assemble a RAG (retrieval‐augmented generation) vector store from these tables, you would index on the Literal plus ETYP plus aggregation level, and you’d store the dimensional metadata and human‐readable “Meaning” to inform downstream queries and prompts.

The table excerpt defines two “STRU” parameters—UNIT and SCHH—that control graphical representation of structural‐analysis results (length scaling and text sizing) when you select a representation (REPR) other than the default diagram (DIAG). Each parameter (listed in the “Item” column) offers several literal inputs, each explained in “Description,” together with the physical “Unit” and the software “Default” code or numeric value.

1. UNIT (Scaling of Representation Length)  
   • Purpose: Governs how numeric result values having a length dimension (for example, deflections, displacements or any result expressed in length units) are mapped to on‐screen lengths.  
   • Literals / Input options:  
     – DEFA  
       • Default behavior: the largest absolute value of the selected result type is drawn about 2 cm long.  
     – LFAC  
       • Use a user‐provided scaling factor, FACS, for all results with length dimension.  
     – LAST  
       • Inherit the same unit (and scale) as was used for the last input of this result type during the current session.  
     – > 0 (any positive number)  
       • You specify which result‐value corresponds exactly to 1 cm in the plot. E.g. if you enter “10,” then a result value of 10 units-length will render as 1 cm.  
     – < 0 (any negative number down to –999)  
       • You specify approximately how many cm the maximum result value should occupy. The software will round “in an engineering way” so that the largest plotted vector spans roughly that many centimeters.  
     – < –1000 (e.g. –1002.5)  
       • Encodes a multiple of DEFA. For instance, –1002.5 means “use DEFA × 2.5” as the scale factor.  
   • Unit column: “–/cm/LIT” indicates that UNIT can be a literal code (DEFA, LFAC, etc.), a pure scaling factor relating model units to cm, or refer to the last‐used input (LIT).  
   • Default: DEFA  

2. SCHH (Text‐Size of a Type)  
   • Purpose: Controls the font size or presence of designation labels (e.g. node numbers, element IDs) in the graphical output.  
   • Literals / Input options:  
     – NO  
       • No designation text at all.  
     – YES  
       • Display the designation at a software‐preset size.  
     – > 0  
       • A positive numeric value (in cm) sets the text height explicitly.  
   • Unit column: “cm/LIT” denotes either a literal flag (NO/YES) or a size in cm.  
   • Default: 0.16  

Usage notes:  
- Both parameters form part of the representation settings for STRU‐type results: if you do not explicitly set UNIT or SCHH, the program default (DEFA or 0.16 cm) applies based on TYPE and ETYP.  
- These controls allow fine‐tuning of diagrams—scaling arrow lengths or vector plots so they remain visible but not overcrowding, and ensuring text is legible without overlapping.  
- When saving these settings in a REP block (REPR ≠ DIAG), you can mix literal keywords and numeric values as shown. This table signals, in its final column, that all listed options are implemented by the software and ready for selection.

The input table is a compact “data‐dictionary” defining six standardized metadata fields for variables used throughout the RAG-vector-store schema (and in related result dumps and reports). Each row associates a short literal identifier with its semantic role (“Meaning”) and its dimensional characteristic (“Dim.”). Below is a detailed description of its structure and intended use:

1. Columns  
   • Literal  
     – A fixed, uppercase code that appears in exported data files, scripts, or API payloads whenever one of these variable‐metadata fields is referenced.  
   • Meaning  
     – A human‐readable label explaining what each literal actually represents. This is the definition that documentation, UI labels or automated parsers will display.  
   • Dim.  
     – The dimensional category of the field’s content. All entries in this table are marked “–” to indicate they are not numerical quantities with physical dimensions, but rather descriptors or indexes.

2. Rows (Field Definitions)  
   1) NAME  
      • Meaning: “Name of variable”  
      • Use: Holds the canonical identifier or code name of the variable whose value or text is being recorded. Typically used as the primary key when indexing or cross‐referencing results.  
   2) VALU  
      • Meaning: “Value of variable with unit”  
      • Use: Stores a numeric measurement together with its unit string. Parsers should split number vs. unit if further computation is required.  
   3) TEXT  
      • Meaning: “Text of variable”  
      • Use: Captures a purely textual or alphanumeric value when the variable cannot be represented by a single numeric entry. Useful for statuses, categories, or long descriptions.  
   4) SCOP  
      • Meaning: “Scope of variable”  
      • Use: Indicates the contextual scope or applicability of the variable—e.g., global vs. local, per-element vs. per-loadcase. Acts as a filter key when selecting which variables to retrieve.  
   5) COMM  
      • Meaning: “Comment on variable”  
      • Use: Provides free‐form explanatory notes or warnings about the variable’s usage, origin, or any caveats. Often shown in tooltips or extended logs.  
   6) DIMI  
      • Meaning: “Unit of variable as index”  
      • Use: An alternate way to represent a unit or dimensional index, particularly where a short code is needed in place of a full unit string. Enables compact storage and faster lookups in environments that support unit tables.

3. Contextual Role in RAG/Vector Store  
   – These six metadata fields form the backbone of how any variable’s metadata is structured in the broader RAG ecosystem. Whenever a result or property is stored—whether it’s a cross‐sectional moment, a material constant or a life‐cycle-assessment metric—its associated NAME, VALU (or TEXT), SCOP, COMM and DIMI entries ensure consistent indexing, retrieval and display.  
   – Downstream components (e.g., report generators, visualization modules or machine-learning pipelines) rely on these literals to automate unit-aware computations, enforce scope constraints, or surface user comments without needing bespoke parsing logic for each new variable type.

4. Dimensional Column (“Dim.”)  
   – All entries show “–” to indicate that these fields themselves do not carry a physical dimension. Instead, they describe or annotate other data that will usually be dimensional (e.g., forces in kN, lengths in m, plastic moments in kNm).  
   – When integrating with tables of numerical results (for beams, springs, life-cycle metrics, etc.), the VALU and DIMI fields serve as the bridge between raw numbers and their correct SI or custom unit representations.

By defining these six literals and their roles in one central table, the RAG-vector-store design achieves:  
   • Uniform metadata handling across heterogeneous result types  
   • Simplified parser logic (always expect the same six keys for every variable)  
   • Clear separation between numeric data and descriptive context, facilitating both human reading and automated processing.

The table under discussion is a concise three-column reference that defines four of the possible literals for the STRU TYPE field used in result filtering and organization (for example, when populating a RAG-style vector store with structural analysis outputs). Each row associates a short code (“Literal”) with its full description (“Meaning”) and indicates whether the quantity carries a physical dimension (“Dim.”). In this snippet all of the entries are dimensionless, so each “Dim.” field is simply marked with a hyphen.

1. Table structure  
   • Column 1, “Literal,” contains the abbreviated identifier that will appear in the STRU TYPE parameter.  
   • Column 2, “Meaning,” gives a human-readable description of what structural entity or grouping that identifier corresponds to.  
   • Column 3, “Dim.” shows the engineering unit for each item; in these four cases the values are purely organizational labels and carry no numeric dimension, hence “–”.

2. Row-by-row breakdown  
   – AXIS  
     • Literal: AXIS  
     • Meaning: “Structural axis”  
     • Dim.: –  
     • Interpretation: When STRU TYPE is set to AXIS, results are aggregated or displayed along the main geometry axes of the structure. This is typically used to extract sectional or axis-aligned summaries (for instance, forces or displacements along a principal frame line).  
   – GLN  
     • Literal: GLN  
     • Meaning: “Structural lines along axis”  
     • Dim.: –  
     • Interpretation: GLN refers more specifically to individual line elements (finite elements of type line or beam) that lie on a defined structural axis. Use this code to isolate data for those linear elements only.  
   – XS  
     • Literal: XS  
     • Meaning: “Beam elements along axis”  
     • Dim.: –  
     • Interpretation: XS is even more narrowly focused: it selects beam-type elements that run parallel to a chosen axis. This is useful when you want to examine bending moments, shear forces, or other beam-specific results on a single alignment.  
   – GAXP  
     • Literal: GAXP  
     • Meaning: “Placements”  
     • Dim.: –  
     • Interpretation: GAXP stands for “placements,” which generally denotes groups of elements ranked by their spatial location or assignment to a placement set. In many structural CAD or FEM workflows, placements define how component parts or substructures are positioned within a larger assembly.

3. Contextual usage in RAG vector stores  
   • When ingesting a finite-element or structural analysis database, each output record can be tagged with its STRU TYPE literal.  
   • Queries against the vector store can then be formulated to retrieve, for example, all beam-element results on axis X (i.e. STRU TYPE = XS) or the full set of structural lines (STRU TYPE = GLN).  
   • Because these entries are dimensionless, they serve purely as categorical filters; the actual numerical information (forces, moments, displacements) appears in separate columns or metadata fields.

In summary, this table is a quick-reference for four category identifiers used in structural result processing. All four serve to partition the model output at different levels of geometric or organizational granularity—axis, line, beam-element, or placement—without introducing any new physical units.

This table defines a set of universal result‐reporting fields (literals) that appear in the output of structural‐analysis programs, indicating basic identifiers, grouping attributes and geometric references. Each row corresponds to one literal (column name), its human‐readable meaning, the element‐type or result‐category flags in which it is available, and—where applicable—its physical dimension.

1. Column Layout  
   • Literal: the abbreviated field name used in result files  
   • Meaning: an English description of what the field represents  
   • B D S T C Q V R E: nine availability flags marking whether the field can appear for each of nine result categories or element‐type groups (a “*” means “available,” “–” means “not supported”)

   • ENO (Element number)

   • GRP (Group number)  
     – Assigns each element to a user‐defined primary group  
     – Available in B, S, T, C, Q categories; not in D, V, R, E

     – Bitmask or list indicating every secondary group to which the element belongs

3. Dim.  
   – The physical dimension or unit associated with the field’s value. A dash (“–”) indicates a dimensionless or purely categorical attribute.

Detailed Field Descriptions:

• ENO  
  – Element number  
  – Unique identifier for the kinematic constraint entry.  
  – Dim.: –  

• GRP  
  – Group numbers  
  – One or more group codes to which this constraint belongs, enabling bulk operations or selective retrieval by group.  
  – Dim.: –  

• KINL  
  – Kind of kinematic constraint  
  – Categorical literal that specifies the type (e.g. hinge, slider, fixed link). Used by solver routines to apply appropriate boundary equations.  
  – Dim.: –  

• NOD1  
  – Coupled node  
  – The “moving” or dependent node whose degrees of freedom are constrained.  
  – Dim.: –  

• NOD2  
  – Reference node  
  – The “master” or independent node that NOD1 follows according to the constraint definition.  
  – Dim.: –  

• COOX  
  – Direction  
  – Indicates the coordinate direction(s) affected (e.g. 1=X, 2=Y, 3=Z or combinations).  
  – Dim.: –

  – Distance  
  – Offset distance between NOD1 and NOD2 along the specified direction(s). Even if expressed in length units, this table marks it dimensionless “–” since it may be normalized internally.  
  – Dim.: –

  – Factor for intermediate nodes  
  – A weighting coefficient applied when the constraint involves interpolation or distribution among several intermediate nodes.  
  – Dim.: –

  – Equation of explicitly defined kinematic constraints  
  – A user‐defined formula (string) that can override or extend the basic DIST/FACT approach. Typically stored as text and parsed by the solver’s constraint handler.  
  – Dim.: –

  – Original kind of kinematic constraint from database  
  – Retains the raw category or legacy code as it was imported, before any post-processing or auto-correction.  
  – Dim.: –

• Indexing Keys: “Literal” values (ENO, GRP, KINL, etc.) serve as field names for embedding extraction or text indexing.  
• Semantic Retrieval: The “Meaning” descriptions guide the generation of query-specific prompts or filters (e.g. “find all hinge constraints in group 5”).  
• Dimensional Filtering: Though most fields are dimensionless here, downstream logic may apply unit checks or conversions if DIST were re‐labeled with length units.  
• Constraint Assembly: At solve time, the system pulls NOD1, NOD2, COOX, DIST, FACT, and (optionally) EQUA to build the constraint matrix. KINL and KINI steer the selection of solver routines and record provenance.  
• Version Control & Traceability: KINI and GRP allow users and automated agents to trace constraints back to their source or phase in a multi-stage design process.

By clearly mapping each literal to its role, the table ensures consistency between the user interface, database storage, and solver ingestion—an essential foundation for reliable, high-performance RAG-enabled engineering workflows.

1. Columns

   • Meaning  
     – A plain-English description of what that code stands for.  
   • Dim.

By standardizing on these five literals, the table ensures that every element can carry a minimal set of descriptive and interoperable properties, without introducing any unit-based complexities. This design supports both automated workflows (e.g., RPC-based attribute retrieval) and manual QC checks (e.g., verifying that every beam has an associated BEAM reference and BIM GUID).

In summary, this simple five‐column table is the cornerstone for mapping raw structural analysis outputs into a form that RAG retrieval systems can index, filter, and join—enabling sophisticated queries such as “give me all mid‐span bending results for beams with pinned ends” or “find the cross‐section coordinates associated with node 1024.”

This table defines a set of “literals” (short keyword codes) that can be appended to structural‐analysis result requests or RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) queries. Each literal controls a particular aspect of the output or serves as a filter flag. Because these codes are used in combination with element‐type qualifiers (ETYP), cross‐section identifiers, material numbers, etc., it’s important for any vector‐store or retrieval system to understand their exact semantics and units.  

Overall structure  
• Columns  
  – Literal: the exact code you would include in a query or data-extraction call.  
  – Meaning: a concise English description of what the code represents.  
  – Dim.: the physical unit (if any) in which the value is reported. A dash (–) denotes a dimensionless or logical flag.  

• Rows: nine distinct literals  

Detailed entries  
1. MAXE  
   • Meaning: “Maximum element-number per element type per load case.”  
   • Dim.: – (dimensionless)  
   • Usage: helps identify the highest indexed element within each ETYP/NUMN group for a given load case. Useful when iterating over or bounding element sets.  

2. SETL  
   • Meaning: “Existing elements per element type.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: returns a count of how many elements of each type (e.g., BEAM, TRUS, QUAD) are present in the model or per load case.  

3. ACTI  
   • Meaning: “Group is activated.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: logical flag (0/1) indicating whether the specified element group is active in the current analysis stage or load case.  

4. OUTP  
   • Meaning: “Group with output.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: logical flag indicating whether results have been requested for that group.  

5. LINE  
   • Meaning: “Material-linear calculated.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: indicates that linear material behaviour was assumed in this analysis pass.  

6. HW  
   • Meaning: “Level of groundwater.”  
   • Dim.: m  
   • Usage: reports the elevation of the groundwater table relative to the model’s datum.  

7. CS  
   • Meaning: “Construction stage.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: integer or code identifying which construction or load stage the results belong to.  

8. FCS  
   • Meaning: “Stiffness factor.”  
   • Dim.: –  
   • Usage: multiplier applied to element stiffness (for staged construction, pre-stress, reduction factors, etc.).  

9. ETOT  
   • Meaning: “Total energy.”  
   • Dim.: MPa  
   • Usage: the strain-energy density or integrated energy measure for the element or group, often used in damage or performance checks.  

Contextual integration  
• In the broader STRU/DIAG framework, each of these literals can appear alongside:  
  – ETYP (element type: BEAM, QUAD, SPRI, etc.)  
  – TYPE (result type: forces, moments, displacements)  
  – MTO qualifiers (MTOT, MTOE, MTOM, …) or MLCA/MLCT for life‐cycle data  
• A query might look like:  
    “REPR=OUTP; ETYP=BEAM; MTO=MTOT; MAXE; CS=2”  
  which would retrieve the maximum beam‐element index in construction stage 2, limited to those beams with output requested and summed total values.  

By indexing these literals and their definitions in your vector store, you enable precise, atomized retrieval of structural‐analysis metadata.

The table below defines a small set of “group-level” literals (identifiers) used in the structural analysis environment. Each row associates a short code (the literal), its human-readable meaning, and the physical or logical dimension (if any). These group attributes can be part of a larger result-type schema (STRA, FILL, ETYP, TYPE, etc.) when you are extracting data for a RAG/vector store or any post-processing:

1. Literal Column  
   • This is the code you will see in result datasets, scripts or API calls. It is always three or four characters long and in uppercase.  

2. Meaning Column  
   • A concise English description of what the code stands for. This should be used to label your fields in a more user-friendly way in documentation or user interfaces.  

3. Dim. Column  
   • The “dimension” column shows units of measure or “–” if the value is dimensionless. In this particular table, all entries are dimensionless, as they represent identifiers, text strings or stage indices rather than physical quantities.

Detailed Breakdown of Each Literal

• ENR  
  – Meaning: “Id of group”  
  – Dimension: –  
  ENR is an integer or index that uniquely identifies a group of structural elements (e.g., a load group, material group or element grouping for output organization). This is the primary key when you join group-level data to element-level results.

• NAME  
  – Meaning: “Description”  
  – Dimension: –  
  This is a free-text field that gives a human-readable name or label to the group. For example, “Primary Beams,” “Stage 2 Concrete,” or “Wind Load Combination.” It helps users quickly understand the purpose or contents of the group.

• CSA  
  – Meaning: “Construction stage begin”  
  – Dimension: –  
  CSA is the starting construction stage index. In a phased construction analysis, you may assign each group a range of stages during which it is active. CSA marks the first stage when this group’s elements are “turned on” or come into action.

• CSE  
  – Meaning: “Construction stage end”  
  – Dimension: –  
  CSE is the ending construction stage index. It indicates the last stage during which the group remains active before being “turned off” or deactivated in later phases. Together, CSA and CSE define the life-span of a group.

• SET0  
  – Meaning: “Selected elements per element type”  
  – Dimension: –  
  This literal holds flags or counts that describe which element types (e.g., beams, shells, solids) are included in this group. Internally, it may be encoded as a bitmask or a small integer where each bit corresponds to a specific element type (ETYP). It facilitates quick filtering of results by type within each group.

How This Table Is Used in Context  
- When exporting or querying structural results, you often specify TYPE (result type), ETYP (element type), STRU (structure type) and possibly FILL or REPR (representation).  
- If you request group-level aggregates—such as total forces, mass, reinforcement lengths, life-cycle assessment values—the system will use ENR to index those aggregates and attach NAME for readability.  
- CSA/CSE let you partition your results by construction stage, a critical feature in staged construction analysis, demolition, or phased loading.  
- SET0 can be used in conjunction with ETYP filters to extract only beams, cables, boundaries, etc., that belong to a particular group.

By mapping these literals into your RAG/vector schema, you can build rich query interfaces:  
- “Show all groups active in stage 3” → filter CSA ≤ 3 ≤ CSE  
- “List group names with beam elements” → SET0 bitmask check + ETYP = BEAM  
- “Fetch group description for group 12” → ENR = 12 → return NAME  

This description should allow you to index, annotate, and retrieve group-level metadata efficiently in your vector store, ensuring that both human users and downstream algorithms can interpret the structural analysis output correctly.

The table is part of the life-cycle assessment (LCA) result definitions and shows, for each LCA metric (the “Literal”), its human-readable meaning, the aggregation levels at which that metric can be reported, and its physical dimension (“Dim.”). An asterisk (“*”) in a column means “available at this aggregation level”; a dash (“–”) means “not available.” Below is a detailed breakdown.

1. Columns  
  • Literal: The internal identifier for the metric.  
  • Meaning: A short description of what the metric represents.  
  • T, P, M, N, G, H, R, S, Y, Z, D, E: Twelve aggregation-level flags corresponding to:  
 – T: Total values (MLCT)  
 – P: Values per phase (MLCA)  
 – M: Values per material (MLCM)  
 – N: Values per material & phase (MLPM)  
 – G: Values per group (MLCG)  
 – H: Values per group & phase (MLPG)  
 – R: Values per secondary group (MLCS)  
 – S: Values per secondary group & phase (MLPS)  
 – Y: Values per structural member (MLCY)  
 – Z: Values per structural member & phase (MLPY)  
 – D: Values per secondary group & design element (MLCD)  
 – E: Values per secondary group & design element & phase (MLPD)  
  • Dim.: The physical or reporting unit of the metric.

2. Rows (Metrics)  
  • MCO2  
 – Meaning: “Global Warming Potential Mass CO2 equivalent.”  
 – Aggregation: Available at every level (T through E all “*”).  
 – Dim.: tCO2  
  • MASS  
 – Meaning: “Mass of material.”  
 – Aggregation: Available at every level (T through E all “*”).  
 – Dim.: t  
  • VOLU  
 – Meaning: “Volume of material.”  
 – Aggregation: Available at every level (T through E all “*”).  
 – Dim.: m³  
  • PHTX  
 – Meaning: “Designation of phase.”  
 – Aggregation: Only at the alternating columns (P, N, H, S, Z, E): every other level, indicated by “*” in columns P, N, H, S, Z, and E; absent in T, M, G, R, Y, D.  
 – Dim.: – (no physical unit)  
  • MDIM  
 – Meaning: “Dimension of Global Warming Potential per phase.”  
 – Aggregation: Only at the material level (column M has “*”); all other levels are “–.”  
 – Dim.: * (unitless or context-dependent)

3. Interpretation and Usage  
  • By consulting this table, an application or user can discover which LCA metrics are reportable at which granularity. For instance, if you need total CO₂ emissions you query MCO2 at “T”; if you want CO₂ broken down by material and phase, you query MCO2 at “N.”  
  • PHTX (phase designation) is only meaningful in contexts where phases are defined (per-phase or per-group & phase, etc.), so it’s unavailable at pure “total” or pure “by material” levels.  
  • MDIM only makes sense when you look at materials in isolation, hence its availability only at column “M.”  
  • The Dim. column tells downstream systems how to label charts, tables, or units in reports.

This structured mapping ensures that any RAG-backed vector store or query interface can dynamically adapt which metrics to fetch or display based on the user’s requested aggregation level.
