This table defines the parameters controlling how cross‐sectional and beam results are graphically or textually represented in the RAG‐enabled viewer. It consists of eight configurable “Items,” each with a short description, an allowed unit type (all are literals, except UNIT and SCHH), and a default value. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Literal that selects which physical quantity or result field is to be displayed (e.g. stresses, reinforcement, temperatures, strains). The full list of valid TYPE keywords appears in the subsequent tables (RFFC, RFFT, RFKP, …, RFMT, RFSS, etc.).  
   • Unit: LIT (string literal)  
   • Default: “*” (no filtering by TYPE)

2. ETYP  
   • Description: Filters display to one or more element types. Valid element‐type literals are:  
     – C (CROS – cross section)  
     – B (BEAM – beam elements)  
     – D (DSLN – design elements)  
     – E (SIR – external beam section)  
     – X (EXPL – explicitly defined internal forces)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (all element types)

3. RTYP  
   • Description: Filters by result‐calculation type. Valid RTYP literals:  
     – N (NONL – nonlinear results from AQB)  
     – C (COMP – nonlinear from COMPOSITE)  
     – F (FIBE – material‐point results from TALPA)  
     – L (LINE – linear elastic stresses)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (all result types)

4. STYP  
   • Description: Filters by cross‐section element subtype. “ALL” selects every section element. Other STYP literals include profiles (PROF), beam tendons (BTEN), design‐element tendons (DTEN), etc.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: ALL

5. REPR  
   • Description: Controls the graphical/text representation mode. Allowed values (all prefixed by “D”):  
     – DTXT: text printed at each point  
     – DVEC: arrows/vectors at single points (drawn in local x‐direction)  
     – DLIN: line plots along thin‐walled or contour edges  
     – DIAG: diagram bars or charts  
     – DLST: tabular text listing  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (use default from STRU REPR)

6. FILL  
   • Description: If a closed contour (e.g. polygonal cross section) is drawn, FILL governs whether and how it is shaded. See record STRU FILL for patterns.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO

7. UNIT  
   • Description: Global scale factor for all length‐based representations (vectors, diagram bars, line‐thickness). Overrides per‐TYPE default scaling found in STRU UNIT.  
   • Unit: – /cm / LIT (dimensionless or in cm units)  
   • Default: DEFA (use default scaling)

8. SCHH  
   • Description: Text‐height (in cm) used for any DTXT or DLST labels. Can be overridden via STRU SCHH.  
   • Unit: cm / LIT  
   • Default: 0.16

Additional Notes (context from “AND, LC” instructions):  
- Only sections defined through the LC record appear in the cross‐section view.  
- Single‐point values (e.g. stress points) are rendered as local‐x vectors (DVEC).  
- Thin‐walled or solid‐element edges display their values as lines (DLIN).  
- Unless ETYP, RTYP or STYP explicitly restricts a TYPE, the chosen TYPE entry applies universally.  
- For combined material‐and‐reinforcement stresses (TYPE = RFSS), both are drawn together and reinforcement stresses are auto-scaled to match material stress ranges.  
- Internal forces/moments for beam sections must be pre‐calculated (AQB, STAR2, ASE, TALPA, SIR) unless ETYP = EXPL is used to supply explicit values.

Below is a structured description of the input‐table excerpt you provided.  In your RAG/vector‐store vocabulary this table defines one of the possible “TYPE” entries (here the literal SECT) and documents for which cross‐section‐ or beam‐element definitions it may be requested, and in which units.  

1.  Overall Purpose of the TABLE  
    •  This table is part of the “CROS” (cross‐section) input family.  It lists the “Literal” codes you can supply in the TYPE field when you want the program to compute or display a given set of cross‐sectional results.  
    •  Each row associates a short text code (“Literal”) with  
       –  A human‐readable definition (“Meaning”)  
       –  Flags showing for which element types (ETYP) it is valid  
       –  The physical dimension or units (“Dim”) of the quantity you will get back.  

2.  Column‐by‐Column Explanation  
    1) Literal  
       •  The exact keyword you type into the TYPE column of your CROS or LC record.  
       •  Here: “SECT”  
    2) Meaning  
       •  A brief description of what the program will compute and display when you request this TYPE.  
       •  For SECT: “Main section values” – i.e. the set of geometric and stiffness properties of a cross section.  
       •  The sub‐items A, Ay, Az, It, Iy, Iz, Iyz, ys, zs, ycs, zcs, EM, GM, gam indicate exactly which values are returned:  
         –  A  : Cross‐sectional area  
         –  Ay, Az : First moments of area about the local z‐ and y‐axes  
         –  It : Torsional constant (polar moment or Saint‐Venant constant)  
         –  Iy, Iz : Second moments of area about y‐ and z‐axes  
         –  Iyz : Product of inertia  
         –  ys, zs : Coordinates of shear center in the local y–z plane  
         –  ycs, zcs : Coordinates of the centroid (centroidal axis)  
         –  EM : Bending stiffness E·I (for both principal axes)  
         –  GM : Shear‐center torsional stiffness G·It  
         –  gam : Warping constant (when applicable)  
    3) ETYP  
       •  Five sub‐columns labelled C, B, D, E, X, corresponding to the valid element‐type letters:  
         C = CROS (cross‐section),  
         B = BEAM,  
         D = DSLN (design element),  
         E = SIR (external beam),  
         X = EXPL (explicit internal‐force input).  
       •  A “*” under an ETYP column means this TYPE is available when you use that element type.  A dash “–” means it is not.  
       •  In our row SECT, only the C column bears “*”, so SECT is valid for CROS definitions, and not for beam (B), design (D), external beam (E) or explicit (X).  
    4) Dim  
       •  The physical units (or “dimension”) of the returned values.  
       •  A “*” is shown here, meaning that the table row encompasses multiple sub‐quantities of differing units (areas in cm² or mm², moments in cm⁴ or mm⁴, lengths in cm or mm, stiffness in kN·cm², etc.).  The program will automatically attach the correct unit to each sub‐item.  

3.  How It Fits into the Workflow  
    •  Before you can call TYPE=SECT, you must have defined a cross‐section via record LC (or CROS).  
    •  Unless you explicitly restrict ETYP via another field, SECT will apply to all cross‐section‐type definitions.  
    •  During “REPR DSTR” (graphical cross‐section display) this SECT request causes the program to compute and overlay all of the main geometric and stiffness properties.  

4.  Notes on Context from the Extended Text  
    •  The broader CROS facility also supports other TYPE codes (for example RFSS, RFKP, RFFT, etc.), each of which has its own table row with its own ETYP‐availability and dimensional units.  
    •  Some TYPEs produce vector drawings (e.g. local‐x stress vectors at discrete points) or line‐plots along thin‐walled sections (contour plots).  SECT simply outputs scalar section properties.  
    •  If you ever use ETYP=EXPL (explicit internal forces), you may also overlay the explicit bending‐ and axial‐resultants on your section.  SECT by itself, however, just reports the geometry and stiffness.  

In summary, this single‐row table defines how to request—and what you get—when you set TYPE=SECT in your cross‐section input.   It is valid only for CROS elements, and returns a bundle of geometric and stiffness quantities in their native units.

The input table defines a set of “TYPE” literals that can be requested when plotting or extracting cross‐section and beam results in a structural‐analysis post–processor (e.g. AQB, COMPOSITE, TALPA, SIR).  Each row associates

  – A two‐ to five‐character code (Literal)  
  – A descriptive Meaning  
  – A five-column ETYP flag block (C, B, D, E, X) showing which element types the result may be applied to  
  – A Dimensional unit for that result  

Columns and flags  
-------------  
• Literal  
  The short keyword used as TYPE in the data input.  
• Meaning  
  A plain‐language label explaining what the literal stands for.  
• ETYP (C B D E X)  
  * C = Cross‐section (CROS)  
  * B = Beam elements (BEAM, SIR)  
  * D = Design elements (DSLN)  
  * E = External beam section (SIR)  
  * X = Explicit definition (EXPL)  
  A star (*) under a given column means the TYPE is valid for that element type. A dash (–) means it is not.  
• Dim.  
  The physical unit in which the result is reported (e.g. m², MPa, cm²).  

Context of use  
-------------  
• Unless overridden by an explicit ETYP / RTYP / STYP selection, every TYPE in this list may be requested globally.  
• Results on single points (such as fiber‐beam points) appear as vectors along the local x‐axis; along thin‐walled or solid‐contour elements they appear as line‐plotted values.  
• During graphical output (REPR DSTR), these TYPE values are drawn together with any cross‐section geometry.  
• If you wish to bypass the FE‐computed internal forces and supply your own, choose ETYP = X (“EXPL”) and mark the row with a ‘Z’ in your input.

   • SGNT

   • TAU

The input table defines six key parameters for controlling how structural data (nodes, boundary‐forces, moments, etc.) are graphically represented in the STRU record. Each parameter is identified by an “Item” name, accompanied by a brief description, its unit of measure, and a default setting. Below is a detailed, self-contained explanation of each entry:

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Indicates the specific kind of quantity to be drawn or tabulated. In a node-based context this might be forces, moments, displacements or constraint reactions. The actual allowable “literals” (string tokens) for TYPE are defined elsewhere (e.g. CMX, CMY, CMZ, CMB for kinematic constraint moments; E, EX, EY for boundary‐force components; S_DR for inter-storey rotation after eigen/earthquake analysis; HRRZ for impedance after non-linear steps, etc.).  
   • Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   • Default: “*” (asterisk, meaning “all available types”)

2. TOTA  
   • Description: Specifies how multiple segment or edge‐based line values are combined into a single graphical diagram. Although the “TOTA” sum‐mode is noted as “not yet supported” for some contexts, the following modes are defined in anticipation:  
     ­ “–” : draw each segment’s line representation independently (normal mode).  
     ­ CONS : collapse the shape to a constant‐height form (average value).  
     ­ TRAP : draw an average in trapezoidal form (linearly varying across the element).  
     ­ PAIR : generate a force‐couple result for positive vs. negative excursions.  
     ­ GENE : compute a single resultant (total) quantity for the entire entity.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “–” (the ordinary per‐segment diagram)

3. REPR  
   • Description: Selects the overall style of representation. Two primary modes are defined:  
     ­ DIAG : diagram (bar/arrow/line) depiction of the quantity.  
     ­ DSTR : “structure” mode, where results are overlaid directly on the finite‐element model geometry (see record STRU REPR for details).  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (all representation types allowed, or automatic choice)

4. FILL  
   • Description: Determines whether closed‐area fills (shading, hatching, color blocks) are used when drawing regions or polygons. The actual fill patterns and colors are specified in the STRU FILL record.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO (no fill)

5. UNIT  
   • Description: Provides a scaling factor for diagram lengths or arrow sizes. You may choose a specific numeric scale (e.g. “–/cm” to indicate “units per centimeter”), or link to a literal defined in STRU UNIT (for automatic or predefined scaling).  
   • Unit: –/cm/LIT  
   • Default: DEFA (use the default global scale)

6. SCHH  
   • Description: Sets the text height for any annotations (node numbers, value labels, etc.). The actual font size and style options are controlled in STRU SCHH.  
   • Unit: cm/LIT  
   • Default: 0.16 (centimeters)

Contextual Notes (from the additional text):  
– All quantities associated with nodes or points (displacements, moments, forces) are represented as vectors in the drawing plane; if a vector is oriented nearly perpendicular to the screen, it is shown using a cross or square “end‐cap.”  
– Edge forces (e.g. along beam or shell edges) appear as lines drawn directly on the element boundary.  
– Structural identifiers (node numbers, element IDs) and boundary conditions are plotted using the STRU record settings.  
– After specialized analyses (eigenmodes, earthquake loads, nonlinear static or dynamic runs), additional TYPE literals become relevant (e.g. S_DR for storey rotations, HRRZ for rotational impedance in a hysteresis plot).  
– While TOTA modes beyond “–” are formally defined, some codes may not yet implement all collapse or averaging schemes; when in doubt, use the default “–” to see each segment separately.

Below is a structured, in-depth description of the three-row lookup table, suitable for ingestion into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store. Context from the surrounding documentation (e.g. “values are represented in nodes or points – storey levels,” “forces/moments are drawn as vectors,” etc.) is woven in where it aids understanding.

1. Overall Table Role  
   •  This table defines three summary quantities—total and component base shears—computed at the base of a multi-storey structure.  
   •  In a typical “eigen form” or “earthquake” calculation (e.g. with DYNA) or any static lateral load check, these values are extracted at the ground/storey interface (node or “point” at storey level).  
   •  Each row maps a short literal code (the “Literal” column) to a human-readable meaning and a physical dimension (the “Dim.” column).

2. Column Breakdown  
   – Literal  
     •  A concise alphanumeric key used throughout the analysis output.  It is what the solver prints and what post-processors (or RAG-backed interfaces) look up to fetch descriptions and units.  
     •  Guaranteed unique within this context.  
   – Meaning  
     •  A plain-English description explaining exactly what physical quantity the code represents.  
     •  Should be treated as the canonical definition when displaying or querying for this code.

     •  The unit in which the quantity is measured.

   1) S_PT  
      •  Full Name: Resulting Base Shear in the XY-Plane  
      •  Definition: The vector magnitude of the total lateral force at the base, combining global X and Y components.  In graphic outputs these would be shown as a single/tipped‐vector lying approximately in the plane of the screen.  
      •  Units: kN  
      •  Usage: Often compared to code-specified design base shear or used to check inter-storey drift demands indirectly via shear distribution.

      •  Full Name: Base Shear in Global X  
      •  Definition: The component of the lateral base shear resolved along the global X axis.  In a force diagram, this would appear as a vector lying horizontally (if X is horizontal).  
      •  Units: kN  
      •  Usage: Used to assemble the S_PT vector (via √(S_PX² + S_PY²)) and to check directional (X-only) load cases or combinations (“LC”).  
   3) S_PY  
      •  Full Name: Base Shear in Global Y  
      •  Definition: The component of the lateral base shear resolved along the global Y axis.  
      •  Units: kN  
      •  Usage: Same role as S_PX but for the orthogonal horizontal direction.

 • IRY  – Incremental rotation about Y‐axis, mrad  
 • IRZ  – Incremental rotation about Z‐axis, mrad  

3. Group 2 – Residual Statics (prefix R)  
 Residuals represent out‐of‐balance forces and moments at each node after internal equilibrium checks or at convergence of a non‐linear solution:  
 • RE   – Residual force resultant (vector magnitude), kN  
 • REX  – Residual force component X, kN  
 • REY  – Residual force component Y, kN  
 • REZ  – Residual force component Z, kN  
 • REM  – Residual moment resultant, kNm  
 • REMX – Residual moment component about X, kNm  
 • REMY – Residual moment component about Y, kNm  
 • REMZ – Residual moment component about Z, kNm  

4. Contextual Notes  
 - All “I…” quantities are typically plotted as vectors (single or double tipped arrows) at node locations, with perpendicular directions shown by cross/rectangle symbols.  
 - Residuals may be drawn as status lines along element edges if the force is edge‐bound.  
 - These literals fit into broader families; for example, “CMX,” “CMY,” etc., refer to constraint‐moment components, while “E,” “EX,” “EY,” “TEX” handle boundary forces in global components.  
 - After special analyses (eigenform, earthquake, impedance histograms), additional TYPE codes (e.g., S_DR for story drift, HRRZ for rotational impedance) become available.

By tagging each node with one or more of these literals, a user or a retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) system can efficiently locate and interpret the precise kinematic or static quantity required for post‐processing, visualization, or further automated reasoning.

This table defines the “H-series” of nodal history and dynamic‐response result types used in structural analyses (especially time‐history or eigenmode computations) and is intended for indexing in a RAG vector store. Each row associates a short literal (code) with its full physical meaning and the units in which it is reported. All values appear at nodes (typically storey‐level points) and can be visualized as scalar or vector quantities according to the direction and nature of the result.

1. General Function  
   • Literal: HFUN  
   • Meaning: A user-defined or internally generated general time/history function  
   • Units: –  

2. Displacements  
   • HUX, HUY, HUZ  
   • Meaning: Nodal translational displacement components along global X, Y, Z  
   • Units: millimetres (mm)  

3. Rotations  
   • HURX, HURY, HURZ  
   • Meaning: Nodal rotational displacement (i.e. torsion/rotation) about global X, Y, Z  
   • Units: milliradians (mrad)  

4. Velocities  
   • HVX, HVY, HVZ  
   • Meaning: Time derivatives of translational displacement (velocity) along X, Y, Z  
   • Units: metres per second (m/sec)  

5. Angular Velocities  
   • HVRX, HVRY, HVRZ  
   • Meaning: Time derivatives of rotational displacement (angular velocity) about X, Y, Z  
   • Units: per second (1/sec)  

6. Accelerations  
   • HAX, HAY, HAZ  
   • Meaning: Time derivatives of velocity (translational acceleration) along X, Y, Z  
   • Units: metres per second squared (m/sec²)  

7. Angular Accelerations  
   • HARX, HARY, HARZ  
   • Meaning: Time derivatives of angular velocity (rotational acceleration) about X, Y, Z  
   • Units: per second squared (1/sec²)  

8. Impedances (Dynamic Stiffness)  
   • HRUX, HRUY, HRUZ  
     – Impedance of translational degrees of freedom (1/uX, 1/uY, 1/uZ) at a node  
     – Units: per metre (1/m)  
   • HRRX, HRRY, HRRZ  
     – Impedance of rotational degrees of freedom (1/urX, 1/urY, 1/urZ)  
     – Units: per milliradian (1/mrad)  

Contextual Notes:  
• These H-series results often follow eigenform or earthquake (DYNA) analyses, or non-linear time‐history runs (e.g. TALPA, ASE, HYDRA).  
• Stored values can represent instantaneous nodal states (displacement, velocity, acceleration) or boundary-condition reactions (impedances).  
• In visualizations, translational quantities appear as vector arrows, rotational ones as curved arrows or double‐tipped vectors; out-of-plane directions use crosses/rectangles.  
• Use these literals when querying the RAG vector store to retrieve semantic embeddings of specific dynamic or kinematic node responses.

The input table is a concise lookup of seven “literals” — short alphanumeric identifiers — each tied to a specific physical quantity and its unit of measure (the “Dim.” column). These codes and units are typically encountered in the context of structural‐thermal or hydraulic post-processing (for example, in histogram outputs after nonlinear or dynamic analyses). Below is a detailed description of its structure and contents:

1. Overall Table Structure  
   • Three columns:  
     – Literal: the abbreviated code used in data records or vector‐graphic outputs.  
     – Meaning: the full name of the physical quantity.  
     – Dim.: the unit or dimension in which that quantity is expressed.  

2. Row-by-Row Breakdown  
   – HT  
     • Meaning: Temperature  
     • Dim.: C (degrees Celsius)  
     • Notes: This literal represents nodal or element temperatures in Celsius. Temperature contours or color maps in post-processing would reference HT.  

   – HTK  
     • Meaning: Temperature in Kelvin  
     • Dim.: K (kelvin)  
     • Notes: When absolute temperature (for gas or thermodynamic calculations) is required, HTK provides the same thermal data on the Kelvin scale.  

   – HHN  
     • Meaning: Heat flux  
     • Dim.: W (watts)  
     • Notes: The local heat flux vector magnitude normal to an element face or node, typically in W per area. In thermal boundary‐force notation (see “E, EX, EY” in the larger context), HHN corresponds to the actual rate of thermal energy flow.  

   – HHR  
     • Meaning: Total Heat flux  
     • Dim.: W (watts)  
     • Notes: Represents an integrated or resultant heat flux over a region or entire structure. Often appears in global summaries after eigen-form or earthquake calculations (DYNA) or thermal load studies.  

   – HH  
     • Meaning: Potential height  
     • Dim.: m (meters)  
     • Notes: In hydraulic or flow analyses this is the hydraulic head or potential energy height. It can also denote nodal elevation in geotechnical modules.  

   – HFN  
     • Meaning: Flow quantity  
     • Dim.: l/sec (liters per second)  
     • Notes: Local volumetric flow rate through an interface or boundary. In post-processing graphics, HFN is drawn much like a vector (single‐tip arrow) when projected in-plane, or a cross if perpendicular to the view.  

   – HFR  
     • Meaning: Integral flow quantity  
     • Dim.: l/sec (liters per second)  
     • Notes: A cumulative flow rate (sum over edges or sections). In edge‐force notation it would appear as a status line on the structure’s perimeter.  

3. Contextual Connections  
   • These literals fall under the general category of “structure values of nodes and boundaries” (record STRU) in many finite‐element or boundary‐element pre/post processors.  
   • Related output groups include:  
     – AND, LC: load combinations or results sets.  
     – TOTA (not yet supported for some vector stores).  
     – S_DR, HRRZ: interstorey rotations and impedance measures in dynamic or nonlinear runs.  
   • Representation conventions:  
     – Forces and moments drawn as single/double tipped vectors.  
     – Values normal to the viewing plane use crosses or rectangles.  
     – Edge quantities are rendered as colored status lines.

Queries referencing “HT” or “HFR” can be linked back to their precise physical meaning and unit, enabling accurate filtering, contextual clustering, or visualization directives within an engineering document corpus.

The table shown defines the input parameters for the BEAM-drawing record (often invoked via “STRU BEAM” in a STRU file) and specifies, for each parameter, its meaning, its data type or unit, and its default setting.  In a RAG/vector-store context you would index each row as a distinct field (Item), with subfields for Description, Unit, and Default.

1. Columns  
   • Item: the name of the input parameter.  
   • Description: what the parameter does and, where applicable, what literal values it accepts.  Cross-references (e.g. “see record STRU FILL”) point to other records for more options.  
   • Unit: the kind of value expected—usually a literal (LIT), a length scale (–/cm/LIT), or a height in cm per literal.  
   • Default: the value assumed if you omit the parameter.

2. Rows / Parameters  
   a) TYPE  
     – Description: the “type” of data to be represented when you draw.  It is a literal token that selects among sub-tables of beam-output quantities (e.g. stresses, forces, reinforcement histograms).  See the detailed lists of BEAM TYPE codes (SPTP, SWPT, … AS9, AST9, etc.) later in the manual.  
     – Unit: LIT (literal)  
     – Default: – (no default; TYPE must be provided)  

   b) STYP  
     – Description: selects the element category whose results you want to plot.  Valid literals are:  
       • DSLN – design elements  
       • BEAM – beam elements  
       • SIR  – external beam-section definitions  
       • TRUS – truss-bar elements  
       • CABL – cable elements  
       • SPRI – all spring elements  
       • QTEN – tendons of plane elements  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: BEAM  

   c) REPR  
     – Description: chooses the graphical style of the plot:  
       • DIAG – diagram representation  
       • DSTR – structure (wireframe) representation  
       • (any other literal defined via record STRU REPR)  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: *  (asterisk, meaning “use all available quantities”)  

   d) FILL  
     – Description: indicates whether to fill the cross-section representation or draw only outlines.  The full list of fill patterns is defined by record STRU FILL in the manual.  
     – Unit: LIT  
     – Default: NO  

   e) UNIT  
     – Description: scaling factor for lengths in the diagram (e.g. you can compress or magnify element axes).  Accepted values and formats are detailed in record STRU UNIT.  
     – Unit: – / cm / LIT  
     – Default: DEFA  

   f) SCHH  
     – Description: text-height (in cm) to be used for labels when annotating your beam diagram.  See record STRU SCHH for additional options (font style, auto-sizing, etc.).  
     – Unit: cm / LIT  
     – Default: 0.16  

3. Usage notes  
   – If you invoke BEAM without specifying REPR, FILL, UNIT or SCHH, the default wireframe, no-fill, default scale and a 0.16 cm text height will be used.  
   – For “TYPE,” you must refer to the manual’s extensive list of stress and force codes (e.g. SPTP for principal tensile stress, SCVY for shear force Vy, AS0–AS9 for reinforcement layers, AST0–AST9 for torsional stirrups, etc.).  Each code has its own availability flags depending on element type (B/S/C/T/D) and on which solver produced the results (STAR2, ASE, COMPOSITE, etc.).  
   – Cross-references (e.g. “see record STRU X”) should be followed to retrieve full enumerations of allowed literals, numerical limits and additional semantic constraints.

The input table defines a set of “literals” (result‐type codes) that BEAM can plot for beam, spring, truss/cable, tube, design and tendon elements.  Each row corresponds to one scalar or force‐type quantity and supplies:

• Literal – the 2–5 character code used in the BEAM command  
• Meaning – a brief English description  
• STYP – a seven-position availability mask (columns B, S, C, T, I, D, Q)  
    ­  B = beam elements  
    ­  S = spring elements  
    ­  C = cable or truss elements  
    ­  T = tube elements  
    ­  I = external beam sections (SIR/AQB special)  
    ­  D = design elements  
    ­  Q = tendons of plane elements  
   A “*” in a position means the value is generally available for that element type; a “–” means it is not available; a digit (1, 2, etc.) indicates availability only when that particular auxiliary program (STAR2, ASE, COMPOSITE, etc.) was used to generate the data.  
• Dim. – the physical unit of the quantity (MPa, kN, cm², kN/m, %, days, or “–” for dimensionless).

The table is organized into three logical blocks:

   • SIGV – von Mises stress (N/mm²)

   • SPT  – Principal tensile stress (N/mm²)  
   • SIGU – Uniaxial top stress (N/mm²)  
   • SIGL – Uniaxial bottom stress (N/mm²)  
   • SIGW – Stress in welds (N/mm²)  
   • DECO – Decompression stress (N/mm²)  
   • FACV – Shear reduction factor (dimensionless)  
   • SWMT – Stress sway of normal stress (N/mm²)  
   • SWSM – Stress sway of shear stress (N/mm²)

3. Design stress of stress point (SPT)  
   • SDPT – Minimum stress (N/mm²)  
   • SZPT – Maximum stress (N/mm²)

– To request one of these results from BEAM, you specify its literal in the TYPE field of the BEAM command (often in combination with AND, LC, or other qualifiers).

– Units in the Dim. column must be respected when interpreting or visualizing the plotted curves or histograms.

The table in question defines all of the status‐line output quantities that the BEAM record can draw or print for beam, spring, truss/cable, tube and related element types.  It is intended to be used in conjunction with the STRU and SCHH records (see “record STRU” and “record SCHH”), as well as the filter keywords AND and LC for combinations of load cases.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents.

1. Column “Literal”  
   – A short, unique code (up to four characters) that identifies the quantity.  
   – Examples: SPTP, SWSP, SCVY, AS0, ULMY, SCL, etc.

2. Column “Meaning”  
   – A human‐readable description, often referencing Eurocode clauses when relevant.  
   – For stress outputs it gives the physical meaning (e.g. “Principal tensile stress”), possibly with the unit.  
   – For utilisation or reinforcement it indicates what ratio or area is reported.

3. Column “STYP” (element types)  
   – Seven flags correspond in order to B, S, C, T, I, D, Q, meaning respectively:  
     B = Beam elements  
     S = Spring elements  
     C = Truss and cable elements  
     T = Tube elements  
     I = External beam sections (only stored by program SIR or AQB)  
     D = Design elements  
     Q = Tendons of plate elements  
   – An asterisk “*” means the value is available for that element type; “–” means it is not.  
   – Sometimes a digit (1, 2, …) replaces “*” indicating availability only under a specific post‐processor (STAR2, ASE, COMPOSITE, etc.).

4. Column “Dim.” (Dimension)  
   – The unit in which the quantity is reported:  
     • N/mm² for stresses  
     • “– ” (blank) for forces, moments and utilisation ratios (internal units)  
     • cm² for reinforcement areas  
     • cm²/m for stirrup or torsional reinforcement per unit length  

5. Groups of output quantities  
   a) Design Stresses and Forces (BEAM TYPE literals)  
     • SPTP, SWPT, SWSP: principal tensile, normal‐stress sway, shear‐stress sway, etc.  
     • SNCT, STCT, STSL, SPCC, SCN, SCVY, SCVZ, SCMT, SCMY, SCMZ, SCMB – various normal forces, shear forces, bending and torsional moments, warping moments.  

   b) Stress Summaries  
     • CSHE (τ shear stress), CSGV (von Mises stress).  

   c) Reinforcement Areas (concrete elements only)  
     • AS (total area), AS0…AS9 (individual layers), A0 (minimum total), A0UE/AOQUE (stirrups min. per cut), AST/AST0…AST9 (torsion reinforcement).  

   d) Histograms After Nonlinear Analysis  
     • Additional records generated by FEABENCH, DYNA, HYDRA post‐processors.  

   e) Utilisation Levels for Concrete and Other Materials  
     • VED, TED, SIG2, CSGR, CAS, CASU, CCW, ULT0 – utilisation or stress ratios in concrete.  
     • ULN, ULVY, ULVZ, ULMT, ULMY, ULMZ, ULMB, ULM2 – utilisation for common materials (timber, steel, composites).  
     • SCL, CSGC, CSGT, CSHE – cross‐section class and utilisation levels for non‐concrete materials.

In practice you select one or more of these literals in a BEAM record (e.g. “BEAM,TYPE=SNCT,SCVY,SCMY”) and then plot or list their values along each element.  The STYP column tells the software which element types will actually carry each result; dimensioning ensures correct interpretation of units at plot time.

Below is a breakdown of its structure, column by column, followed by a description of the various groups of literals.

1.  Table‐Columns  
    •  Literal  
       –  The alphanumeric code you use in your BEAM record to select a particular output quantity.  
    •  Meaning  
       –  A short description of the physical or design quantity produced for that literal.  
    •  STYP  
       –  A 7-character bitmask showing for which element categories the quantity is available. The positions correspond to:  
         B = Beam elements  
         S = Spring elements  
         C = Truss/Cable elements  
         T = Tube elements  
         I = External beam sections (SIR/AQB)  
         D = Design elements  
         Q = Tendons of plane elements  
       –  A “*” means the value is printed for that element type; “–” means it is not.  
       –  In addition, numerical flags 1, 2 or the letter C (COMPOSITE) may appear in other tables to indicate storage by STAR2/AQB, ASE, or COMPOSITE, respectively.  
    •  Dim.  
       –  The engineering unit in which the quantity is reported (cm², cm²/m or “–” if dimensionless).

2.  Literal Groups  
    A.  Minimum Reinforcement Areas (cm²)  
       •  A00 … A09  
          –  “Minimum reinforcement layer 0” through “layer 9.”  
          –  Total minimum required steel area in each concrete layer.  
          –  STYP = “*-*-* * –” ⇒ printed for Beams, Cables/Trusses, External sections, Design elements.  

    B.  Shear Design Error (dimensionless)  
       •  ASE  
          –  “Shear design error for all layers.”  
       •  ASE0 … ASE9, ASEA … ASEE  
          –  Layer-specific shear design error from layer 0 up to layer 14 (ASEE = layer 14).  
       •  Unit = “–” (ratio of applied to design shear capacity).  
       •  STYP = “*-*-* * –” ⇒ available for the same element set as above.  

    C.  Maximum Stirrup Reinforcement Including Torsion (cm²/m)  
       •  ASU  
          –  “Maximum stirrup reinforcement (including torsional stirrups).”  
       •  ASU0 … ASU9, ASUA … ASUE  
          –  “Stirrup reinforcement layer 0 through layer 14” (per cut part).  
       •  Unit = cm²/m (area per meter of beam length).  
       •  STYP = “*-*-* * –.”  

    D.  Maximum Stirrup of Minimum Reinforcement (cm²/m)  
       •  A0U  
          –  “Maximum stirrup of minimum reinforcement (including torsional stirrups).”  
       •  A0U0 … A0U9, A0UA  
          –  “Stirrup minimum reinforcement layer 0 through layer 10” (per cut part).  
          –  (If the table extended, it would go through A0UE = layer 14.)  
       •  Unit = cm²/m.  
       •  STYP = “*-*-* * –.”  

3.  Key Points and Usage  
    –  All of these outputs are intended for reinforced-concrete beam design checks (EN 1993-1-1 or similar codes).  
    –  The “shear design error” ASE is the ratio of required to provided shear reinforcement; values >1 indicate under-reinforcement.  
    –  The ASU and A0U families allow you both to examine the actual (ASU) and minimum required (A0U) stirrup areas, layer by layer.  
    –  By combining these literals with the BEAM record’s PRINT options (and with record STRU for element numbering), you can generate per‐element histograms of stresses, forces and design ratios.  
    –  If you need these quantities in a nonlinear post‐processing step (FEABENCH, HYDRA, DYNA or similar), be sure that the solver writes out BEAM histograms via its “nonlinear histogram” option.

This table is part of the BEAM output record set, which the pre‐ and post‐processor uses to plot or extract sectional and reinforcement results on beam-type finite elements. In a RAG (Retrieve–Augment–Generate) vector-store context, each row becomes a document with the fields below, enabling precise filtering by element type, variable name (literal), physical meaning and units.

1.  Columns  
   • Literal: the short code used in the BEAM record.  
   • Meaning: a human-readable description of what the code stands for.  
   • STYP (element applicability mask): seven sub-fields for element classes—B (Beam), S (Spring), C (Truss/Cable), T (Tube), I (Design element), D (Tendon), O (External section via SIR/AQB), Q (Composite code).  
       – ‘‘*’’ means the value is generally available for that element class.  
       – ‘‘–’’ means not available.  
       – ‘‘1’’, ‘‘2’’, ‘‘3’’ indicate availability only when using STAR2/AQB, ASE, or COMPOSITE modules.  
   • Dim. (Dimension): the physical unit of the variable.

2.  Torsional Stirrup Contributions (AST* … ASTE)  
   • ASTA through ASTE represent the cross-sectional area of stirrups in torsion, for layers 10…14 respectively, given per unit cut length.  
   • Availability mask ‘‘*–*–**–’’ shows they’re computed for beams, trusses and tubes but not springs, tendons or external sections.  
   • Units: cm²/m.  

3.  Minimum Stirrup Contributions (A0T0 … A0TE)  
   • A0T0 through A0TE mirror AST* but for the minimum‐required stirrup area for layers 0…14 (per cut part).  
   • Same availability pattern and units (cm²/m).  

4.  Section Geometry & Internal-Force Offsets  
   • HL: lever arm of internal forces (m).  
   • HVMW: shift rule offset included in reinforcement (m).  
   • HVMO: shift rule offset not included in reinforcement (m).  
   • All three are available for beams, trusses and tubes (mask ‘‘*–*–**–’’).  

5.  Bedding (Subgrade) Forces  
   • PA: axial bedding force (EN 1993-1-1 normalization), units kN/m².  
   • PT: lateral bedding force (global coordinate).  
   • PTY: lateral bedding force in local y-direction.  
   • PTZ: lateral bedding force in local z-direction.  
   • These are only stored by ASE (mask ‘‘2––––––’’).  

6.  How to Use in a RAG Pipeline  
   – Index ‘‘Literal’’ as the retrieval key; e.g. a user asks for “torsional stirrup layer 12” → match ASTC.  
   – Filter on STYP to restrict to specific element classes.  
   – Present ‘‘Meaning’’ and ‘‘Dim.’’ fields as metadata for display or downstream processing.  
   – If the retrieval needs only ASE-derived bedding forces, require STYP mask containing “2” in the PA/PT/PTY/PTZ rows.  

7.  Contextual Notes from Additional Text  
   – BEAM draws status lines of beam/spring elements; for full structural plotting of beams, use STRU record in conjunction.  
   – The ‘‘last column’’ (Dim.) tells post-processors how to scale and label axes or tables.  
   – Other BEAM TYPE codes (e.g. SPTP, SWPT, SNCT, SCMY) exist for stresses and internal forces; they follow the same column structure but are not shown here.

By structuring each row as a mini-document with these four fields and a seven-bit element mask, the RAG system can flexibly fetch exactly those beam results (stresses, forces, reinforcement areas) needed for visualization, design checks or further automated processing.

The BEAM output record is used to extract status lines—forces, moments and stresses—of beam and spring elements (including trusses, cables and tubes in some cases). The accompanying table defines each available “literal” (code) that BEAM can produce, gives a short “meaning” for each code, indicates by element type whether that quantity is actually stored, and specifies its physical dimension.

1. Table Structure  
   • Literal: The internal code name for the quantity.  
   • Meaning: A concise description of the mechanical quantity.  
   • STYP: A bit‐mask across seven element categories. A “*” means the value is stored for that element type, a “–” means it is not. The seven positions correspond, in order, to  
     1) B = Beam elements  
     2) S = Spring elements  
     3) C = Truss and cable elements  
     4) T = Tube elements  
     5) I = External beam sections (only by SIR or AQB)  
     6) D = Design elements  
     7) Q = Tendons of plane elements  
   • Dim.: The physical dimension or unit (kN, kNm, kNm², etc.).  

2. Beam‐Force and Moment Quantities  
   • H_N  
     – Meaning: Axial force along the element axis  
     – STYP: * * * – – – – (available for beams, springs, trusses/cables)  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • H_VY  
     – Meaning: Shear force causing transverse bending  
     – STYP: * * – – – – – (beams and springs only)  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • H_VZ  
     – Meaning: Shear force causing principal bending  
     – STYP: * * – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • H_MT  
     – Meaning: Torsional moment about the element axis  
     – STYP: * * – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kNm  
   • H_MY  
     – Meaning: Bending moment in the principal bending plane  
     – STYP: * – – – – – – (beams only)  
     – Dim.: kNm  
   • H_MZ  
     – Meaning: Bending moment in the transverse bending plane  
     – STYP: * – – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kNm  
   • H_MB  
     – Meaning: Warping moment (torsion‐induced warping)  
     – STYP: * – – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kNm²  
   • HMT2  
     – Meaning: Secondary torsional moment (e.g. distortion)  
     – STYP: * – – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kNm  

3. Spring‐Force Quantities  
   • HPTX  
     – Meaning: Spring shear force in global X direction  
     – STYP: – * – – – – – (only springs)  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • HPTY  
     – Meaning: Spring shear force in global Y direction  
     – STYP: – * – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • HPTZ  
     – Meaning: Spring shear force in global Z direction  
     – STYP: – * – – – – –  
     – Dim.: kN  
   • HPTP  
     – Meaning: Spring shear‐force ratio Pt/P (used in some nonlinear analyses)  
     – STYP: – * – – – – –  
     – Dim.: – (dimensionless)  

Notes:  
– Any “*” under STYP indicates that BEAM will output that quantity for the corresponding element type; a dash “–” means it will not.  
– External sections (“I”), design elements (“D”) and tendons (“Q”) rarely appear for these core quantities.  
– This table serves as a legend for interpreting BEAM outputs in subsequent STRU or SCHH records, enabling automated parsing and indexing in a RAG vector store.

The fragment shown is a subsection of the BEAM output‐table definitions, specifically listing a small set of spring-related and stress-related “literals” that the BEAM postprocessor can draw when invoked (see also record STRU, SCHH). BEAM can plot status lines for beam and spring elements and, in combination with STRU, will annotate element numbers and other structural values. The last column in the table (“Dim.”) gives the physical unit associated with each literal; the central block (“STYP”) indicates for which element types the value is stored and available.

1. Column headings  
   – Literal: the short code by which BEAM refers to a particular result quantity.  
   – Meaning: a human-readable label or description of what the literal represents.  
   – STYP: a series of seven positions (B, S, C, T, I, D, Q) that flag availability:  
     • B = beam elements  
     • S = spring elements  
     • C = truss/cable elements  
     • T = tube elements  
     • I = external beam sections (from SIR or AQB)  
     • D = design (D-type) elements  
     • Q = tendon layers in plane elements  
     A star (*) indicates that BEAM will output that literal for the given element type; a dash (–) means it will not.  
   – Dim.: the engineering units in which the numeric result is presented (e.g. kN, kNm, N/mm², cm², etc.), or “–” for dimensionless ratios.

2. Spring-force and spring-moment ratios  
   • HDPP – “Spring force ratio dP/P.” This is a dimensionless measure of incremental to total pre-load in a spring. STYP = “– * – – – – –” means only spring elements produce it; all other element types show a dash.  
   • HSPX, HSPY, HSPZ – “Total of spring forces SPX/SPY/SPZ” in the global X, Y, Z directions, respectively. Units: kN. Only springs (S) carry these.  
   • HPRX, HPRY, HPRZ – “Total of spring moments SPRX/SPRY/SPRZ” about the global X, Y, Z axes. Units: kNm. Again, these are only relevant for springs (STYP = “– * – – – – –”).

3. Stress quantities  
   • HSIG – “Normal stress” (σ). Unit: N/mm². STYP = “* – – – – – –” indicates it is only available for beam elements.  
   • HTAU – “Shear stress” (τ). Unit: N/mm². Also only for beams.  
   • HSGV – “von Mises stress.” Unit: N/mm². Likewise only for beams.

3. Interpretation and usage  
   – If you request BEAM plots for springs (STYP position S), you will see HDPP, HSPX/Y/Z, HPRX/Y/Z. No beam stresses appear because STYP for S is “–” under HSIG, HTAU, HSGV.  
   – If you request beam element stress plots, only HSIG, HTAU and HSGV are available; all the spring-type fields are blank.  
   – The STYP vector can be read left-to-right as B/S/C/T/I/D/Q; for example, a STYP string of “* – * – * * –” would indicate availability on beam, on C-type, on I and D-type elements, but not on springs, tubes or tendons.  
   – Dimensions remind the user to convert or interpret the raw numeric output correctly when generating cross-plots or exporting to a vector store for further RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) indexing.

In summary, this table snippet documents exactly which scalar fields BEAM can output for spring vs. beam elements, what they mean, and the units in which they are reported. It is essential reference material when building a RAG vector store of postprocessing results, ensuring that only valid (available) fields are indexed per element type and that their units are preserved for downstream queries or plotting.

The table shown is a parameter‐definition block used by the Result Viewer (or equivalent post‐processor) to control how QUAD‐element results are selected, formatted, and drawn. It lists eight “items” (parameters), each with a brief description, its data unit or type, and a default value. Below is a row‐by‐row breakdown:

1. TYPE  
   • Description: Specifies which result field is to be displayed (e.g. shear force vx, vy; membrane stress SV; equivalent stress SVU; etc.). The actual list of valid TYPE literals depends on which solver/program produced the QUAD results (e.g. ASE, DYNA, TALPA for internal forces; BEMESS or ASE for elasticity stresses; HYDRA for non‐linear histograms).  
   • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: “–” (none; must be supplied by the user)  
   • Notes: In practice, TYPE picks one of the predefined result names (see the supplementary tables of QUAD TYPE and stress TYPE).  

2. STYP  
   • Description: Chooses the element‐location level for plotting. Three options:  
     – ELEM: use element centers only  
     – NODE: use element nodes only  
     – FULL: combine NODE + ELEM  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (wildcard = both if unspecified)  

3. TOTA  
   • Description: Toggles the “total” (sum) form of line‐type representations (cuts). This is intended for sums of internal forces along a user‐defined cut line.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “–” (off / not used)  
   • Notes: To use this you must also define record NODE TOTA to describe the cut geometry.  

4. AVER  
   • Description: Governs whether contour‐line result jumps at group boundaries are averaged or not. Along group edges (as defined in the STRU record), node values may be discontinuous—AVER = YES forces node values to be averaged across the boundary, while NO leaves the natural jump.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO  

5. REPR  
   • Description: Sets the type of graphical representation. Two main modes:  
     – DIAG: standard diagram (arrows, vectors, etc.)  
     – DSTR: structure‐style rendering (uses STRU record parameters for lines, markers)  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (inherits or chooses automatically if not specified)  
   • Notes: Further refined by record STRU REPR.  

6. FILL  
   • Description: Enables or disables “fill” shading under the diagram or structural representation.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO  
   • Notes: Details such as color or hatch are specified in record STRU FILL.  

7. UNIT  
   • Description: Scaling factor for the length of graphical elements (e.g. arrow lengths, line segments). You may supply a numeric scale or “DEFA” (use program default).  
   • Unit: – / cm / LIT (a slash‐delimited notation indicating either no unit, centimeters, or literal keywords)  
   • Default: DEFA  
   • Notes: Exact syntax and interpretation come from record STRU UNIT.  

8. SCHH  
   • Description: Height of textual annotations in the plot (labels, legends, node numbers).  
   • Unit: cm / LIT  
   • Default: 0.16 (cm)  
   • Notes: Controlled and overridden via record STRU SCHH if needed.  

General Context & Cross‐References  
• Records beginning with STRU (structure) define detailed styling—line widths, colors, patterns—for representations selected by REPR, FILL, UNIT, and SCHH.  
• Records beginning with LC (layer control) let you specify a depth X inside the QUAD thickness for stress evaluations in laminated elements (e.g. glass or timber layers), which then appear under certain TYPE settings.  
• The items TOTA and AVER are currently placeholders in some workflows and may be ignored unless specific cut / averaging behavior is required.  
• After non-linear analysis (ASE), extra TYPE literals (HVX, HVY) appear, representing shear in local directions. These too are filtered through this same table.

The table defines a compact set of “TYPE” codes and their meanings for internal‐force results on 2D QUAD (quadrilateral) shell or plate elements. These result types become available after a finite-element calculation (for example with the ASE solver) and are stored in the RAG vector database. Each entry also carries its physical dimension (per unit length) so that post-processing tools (e.g. MAXIMA, Result Viewer) can interpret, plot or further process the results correctly.

1. General structure  
   • TYPE – a short literal code identifying the result field.  
   • Meaning – human-readable description (always “in local directions,” i.e. axes aligned with the element’s local coordinate system).  
   • Dim. – the physical dimension, showing kN/m for shear and membrane forces or kNm/m for bending moments and twisting.

2. Bending Moments (units: kNm/m)  
   – BM   : Bending moments in local directions (vector‐valued, full bending moment tensor).  
   – MX   : Bending moment component about the local x‐axis.  
   – MY   : Bending moment component about the local y‐axis.  
   – MXY  : Twisting (torsional) moment in the local xy‐plane.

3. Membrane (In‐Plane) Forces (units: kN/m)  
   – N    : Membrane forces in local directions (full membrane force tensor).  
   – NX   : Normal membrane force in the local x‐direction.  
   – NY   : Normal membrane force in the local y‐direction.  
   – NXY  : Shear membrane force in the local xy‐direction.

4. Shear (Transverse) Forces (units: kN/m)  
   The plate-bending (transverse) shear forces are stored in two forms: signed and absolute – the signed values let you track sign conventions and plot sign‐sensitive diagrams; the absolute values feed into envelope‐type design checks (e.g. MAXIMA).  
   – BV   : Shear forces in local directions (vector form, with sign).  
   – VX   : Transverse shear force in the local x‐direction (signed).  
   – VY   : Transverse shear force in the local y‐direction (signed).  
   – AVX  : Absolute value of shear force in local x, |VX|.  
   – AVY  : Absolute value of shear force in local y, |VY|.

3. How it ties into the wider RAG workflow  
   • QUAD TYPE and record STRU control which element-types (thickness, layering) are present, so that e.g. laminated glass or timber layer stresses (via record LC XI) can be extracted later.  
   • Shear forces appear twice (signed vs. absolute) to support both graphical representation and maximum‐envelope extraction (program MAXIMA).  
   • These codes are one subset of many possible “TYPE” literals; others may appear after shell non-linear (HYDRA) or boundary-element (BEMESS) runs, or for stress invariants (SV, SVXI, IS1X, IS2X) and effective depths (DDUS).  
   • Upstream records such as AND or LC may refine what depth or layer is queried; TOTA and AVER remain reserved but unused here.

By standardizing on these “TYPE” codes and dimensions, the RAG system enables consistent data ingestion into vector stores and downstream retrieval for plotting, design checks and automated report generation.

The table is a fragment of the QUAD‐element stress‐result catalog; it defines the literal codes, their semantic meaning and units for two through‐thickness positions in a 2D quadrilateral finite‐element. It is organized into three columns—“TYPE,” “Meaning” and “Dim.”—and into two sub‐sections:

1. In‐depth (at a specified layer within the element thickness)  
2. Upper surface (the top face of the element)

Each row associates a short alphanumeric “TYPE” code with a human‐readable description (“Meaning”) and the physical dimension (“Dim.”). All stress quantities are given in kN/m².

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
1. In‐depth (Xi) stresses  
   (These entries apply at a defined relative depth Xᵢ through the element thickness. Xᵢ is set by record LC_XI.)  

   • HSXI  
     – Plane principal stresses (i.e. the vector of first and second principal stresses combined)  
     – kN/m²  

   • SIXI  
     – Plane stress I (the maximum principal stress in the plane)  
     – kN/m²  

   • SIIX  
     – Plane stress II (the minimum principal stress in the plane)  
     – kN/m²  

   • NSXI  
     – Stresses resolved along the local element axes (normal stresses in local x and y)  
     – kN/m²  

   • SXXI  
     – Stress normal to local x direction  
     – kN/m²  

   • SYXI  
     – Stress normal to local y direction  
     – kN/m²  

   • TXYX

Contextual Notes (from the surrounding documentation):  
- These TYPE codes become active after a non-linear calculation with HYDRA, but there are analogous TYPE codes used after elasticity‐based stress calculations (program BEMESS) or layer-element analyses (program ASE).

This is especially important for layered elements such as laminated glass or timber, where one often needs stresses in individual plies (see AQUA manual, record FLAY).

By indexing each stress quantity under its TYPE code, a RAG (retrieve-and-generate) system can efficiently pull out exactly the stress results needed—whether principal values, local components, or shear in the membrane—at any of the three key depths through the element thickness.

The input table is part of a larger data model used to organize post-processing results for two-dimensional QUAD finite elements—especially stresses computed after linear or non-linear analysis (programs ASE, BEMESS, HYDRA, etc.). In a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) context, it can serve to disambiguate which stress quantity is being referenced when users query the database.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Literal: a short code identifying the stress quantity.  
     – Meaning: a human-readable description.  
     – Dim.: the physical unit of the quantity.  
   • Rows (eight entries) cover upper and lower extreme stresses, shear extremes, and von Mises stresses.

2. Row-by-Row Explanation  
   • SMIU (Upper minimum stresses) – The largest tensile (positive) stress at the upper surface or layer of the QUAD element. Units N/mm².  
   • SMAU (Upper maximum stresses) – The largest compressive (negative) stress at the upper surface. Units N/mm².  
   • SMIL (Lower minimum stresses) – The largest tensile stress at the lower surface or layer. Units N/mm².  
   • SMAL (Lower maximum stresses) – The largest compressive stress at the lower surface. Units N/mm².  
   • TAUM (Minimum shear stresses) – The minimum (most negative) shear stress component within the QUAD element, usually in‐plane shear. Units N/mm².  
   • VSMA (Maximum von Mises stress) – The peak equivalent stress according to the von Mises criterion, computed over thickness. Units N/mm².  
   • VSMU (Upper von Mises stress) – Equivalent von Mises stress evaluated at the upper surface. Units N/mm².  
   • VSML (Lower von Mises stress) – Equivalent von Mises stress evaluated at the lower surface. Units N/mm².

3. Contextual Integration  
   – These “Literal” codes appear in the record TYPE for stress output. Depending on the solver module (ASE for layered shells, BEMESS for elasticity theory), different subsets of these codes become relevant.  
   – QUAD node shear forces are stored twice—once signed (for graphical plotting) and once absolute (for maximum extraction via MAXIMA). Similarly, stresses appear both as signed values (to capture tension vs. compression) and as invariants or equivalents for design checks.  
   – Layered stresses (upper vs. lower) are critical for laminated materials (glass, timber), where internal ply stresses vary through thickness (see the FLAY module in the AQUA manual). Records such as LC XI let users specify a depth within the element for stress evaluation, but the eight codes listed here always refer to the top or bottom face.  
   – All quantities share the dimension N/mm², consistent with common structural‐analysis conventions.  

4. Usage in RAG Vector Store  
   – Index each row as a separate document embedding, with fields {literal, description, unit}.  
   – Link these entries to broader contexts:  
     • QUAD element definitions (record STRU)  
     • Stress‐postprocessing modules (ASE, BEMESS)  
     • Design‐check programs (MAXIMA)  
   – Enable queries such as “What is SMIL?” or “Show all von Mises stress types and units” to retrieve precise definitions and their relationships to analysis workflows.

The table under review is a lookup of output‐field identifiers (the “TYPE” codes) that may appear in quad‐element result lists (e.g. from ASE, DYNA, TALPA, BEMESS or HYDRA runs). Each row associates a short code with its engineering meaning and the physical unit (“Dim.”) in which the quantity is reported. Internally the table is organized into logical groups separated by spacing:

1. Upper and lower reinforcement reserves  
   • ASU    – Upper reinforcement (total area of steel per unit width) [cm²/m]  
   • ASUH   – Upper principal reinforcement [cm²/m]  
   • ASUQ   – Upper transverse reinforcement [cm²/m]  
   • ASUI   – Upper 3rd reinforcement layer [cm²/m]  
   • ASL    – Lower reinforcement [cm²/m]  
   • ASLH   – Lower principal reinforcement [cm²/m]  
   • ASLQ   – Lower transverse reinforcement [cm²/m]  
   • ASLI   – Lower 3rd reinforcement layer [cm²/m]  

2. Stirrup reinforcement  
   • ASSB   – Stirrup reinforcement—cross‐section per unit plan area [cm²/m²]  
   • ASSE   – Stirrup reinforcement per element [cm²]  

3. Shear‐design parameters  
   • TAU0   – Design shear stress τ = V/(b·z) or τ = V/(b·d) [N/mm²]  
   • ZMIN   – Minimum internal lever arm (z) [m]  
   • VEDR   – Utilization ratio max(VED/VRD,max) [–]  
   • VSD    – Maximum design shear force VSD [kN]  
   • COTT   – Maximum cot θ (angle factor for shear‐stress distribution) [–]  

4. Serviceability‐limit strain check (SLS concrete pressure)  
   • CPU    – Maximum top SLS design concrete pressure on tension side [N/mm²]  
   • CPL    – Maximum bottom SLS design concrete pressure on tension side [N/mm²]  

5. Punching‐shear verification results  
   • ISTA   – State of punching force or binary flag (e.g. 0 = safe, 1 = failure) [–]  
   • VTOT   – Total punching shear force acting on critical perimeter [kN]  
   • VPUN   – Reduced (effective) punching force after eccentricity or edge reductions [kN]  
   • IDUS   – Punching‐state identifier (code for punching status) [–]  
   • TXTD   – Textual description or comment on punching check [–]  
   • UTOT   – Length of the first punching perimeter (unreduced) [m]  
   • URED   – Effective (reduced) length of the first punching perimeter [m]  
   • REDO   – Reduction factor for openings or free edges [–]  
   • BETA   – Eccentricity ratio β (for converting eccentric loads to an equivalent central load) [–]  
   • HDUS   – Slab total thickness at punching region [m]  
   • DDUS   – Slab effective depth (distance from compression face to centroid of tension reinforcement) [m]  

How to read and apply these codes  
— In an ASE output file, each QUAD element or node record will carry one or more of these TYPE codes.  
— The “Meaning” column reminds you which structural or design quantity they refer to.  
— The “Dim.” column tells you how to interpret the numeric value (for unit consistency in post-processing).  
— Reinforcement quantities (ASU*, ASL*) are always given per meter of element edge length; ASSB/ASSE give stirrup steel either per plan area or per element; shear and punching results are global per-perimeter or per-section values.  
— SLS and punching sections only appear if the corresponding checks were requested (strain‐based SLS or punching check via HYDRA).  

This mapping is instrumental for any RAG‐style vector store or custom post-processing: it allows queries to resolve a short code like “VSD” into “Maximum design shear force [kN]” and to fetch or convert its values correctly.

This table defines a set of literal parameters used by the RSET (Result Set) and STRU (structure‐plot) records to control how finite‐element or BRIC‐type results are extracted, formatted and displayed.  It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers eight configurable items.

1. TYPE (Unit = LIT; Default = “–”)  
   • A literal code that selects which result quantity or feature is to be represented.  Valid TYPE values are defined in auxiliary tables (see also AND, LC and BRIC).  In a BRIC‐based postprocessor, TYPE might identify stress, strain, displacement, material ID or other scalar/vector fields.  If you have non‐linear analyses from TALPA/ASE, FEABENCH, DYNA or HYDRA, you will find additional TYPE keywords in the program‐specific appendices.

2. STYP (Unit = LIT; Default = “*”)  
   • The element domain in which the result is sampled.  Options:  
     – ELEM: sample at element centers (one result per BRIC element)  
     – NODE: sample at nodes (one result per node)  
     – FULL: combine both NODE and ELEM results  
   “*” instructs the system to use all available sampling locations.

3. TOTA (Unit = LIT; Default = “–”)  
   • When a line‐type result representation is requested (for example, cutting‐plane or section plots), TOTA indicates whether to sum up the results along the cut.  The implementation hook is in record NODE TOTA, but note that this option is not yet used in the current postprocessors.

4. AVER (Unit = LIT; Default = NO)  
   • Relevant only when STYP = NODE and you are plotting group boundaries or contour lines (the same boundaries that are described with STRU).  
     – NO: do not average nodal values across adjacent elements (results will “jump” at element interfaces)  
     – YES: compute the average of all contributing element values at each boundary node for a smooth contour  

5. REPR (Unit = LIT; Default = “*”)  
   • Selects the visual representation style.  Options:  
     – DIAG: a diagrammatic view (e.g. bar, arrow or glyph)  
     – DSTR: a full structural outline (wireframe or mesh overlay)  
   If “*” is specified, both representations will be generated.  (See also record STRU REPR for more detail.)

6. FILL (Unit = LIT; Default = NO)  
   • Determines whether closed shapes or regions in the structural view are rendered with solid or patterned fill.  See record STRU FILL for available fill patterns and hatch styles.

7. UNIT (Unit = –/cm/LIT; Default = DEFA)  
   • A scaling factor that converts the physical length units of the representation into image units (centimeters) or abstract “literal” units.  “DEFA” uses the default scale currently set in the postprocessor.  To override, specify a numeric scaling value followed by /cm or /LIT.

8. SCHH (Unit = cm/LIT; Default = 0.16)  
   • Specifies the height of text annotations (legends, labels, values) in centimeters per literal unit.  A positive real number controls font size; the default 0.16 produces labels that are legible without overwhelming the structural view.  Consult record STRU SCHH for alternate sizing conventions.

Additional notes:  
• The items TOTA and AVER are placeholders for future cut‐summation and nodal averaging features—currently they have no effect if used.  
• When plotting material or result volumes (e.g. component IDs or color‐mapped stress fields), the actual geometry is driven by record STRU, which references the same parameter names under its own heading.  
• Beyond this table, look to the BRIC TYPE appendix and the RSET chapter (3.34) for complete lists of TYPE literals, histogram settings and non‐linear‐analysis flags.

The table shown is part of the RSET (Result Sets) section in a larger finite-element data schema. It defines a compact list of stress-related record types, each identified by a short “Records” code, a human-readable “Meaning” and the associated physical “Dim.” (dimension). Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. General Context  
   • RSET is the namespace for result-type records generated after an analysis step.  
   • These records are always reported in global Cartesian coordinates.  
   • All stress magnitudes carry the SI unit kN/m².  
   • Upstream in the data flow, you will sometimes see references to AND or LC (load cases), and after post-processing programs like TALPA/ASE or non-linear solvers (FEABENCH, DYNA, HYDRA). But RSET slices out the final stress output.  

2. Record Codes and Their Interpretations  
   – NS  
     • Meaning: The “spatial” stress record, often labeled NS, is a composite. It can be used to request all three normal stresses plus the three shear stresses in one go. Internally it flags that the software should output SX, SY, SZ, TXY, TXZ, TYZ in a single dataset.  
     • Dim.: kN/m²  

   – SX, SY, SZ  
     • SX: Normal stress σx in the global X-direction.  
     • SY: Normal stress σy in the global Y-direction.  
     • SZ: Normal stress σz in the global Z-direction.  
     • Dim.: kN/m² each  

   – TXY, TXZ, TYZ  
     • TXY: Shear stress τxy in the plane formed by the global X and Y axes.  
     • TXZ: Shear stress τxz in the plane formed by the global X and Z axes.  
     • TYZ: Shear stress τyz in the plane formed by the global Y and Z axes.  
     • Dim.: kN/m² each  

3. Notes on Usage  
   • The literal NS can be used when you want a full third-order stress tensor field in one record.  
   • SX/SY/SZ and TXY/TXZ/TYZ allow selective output, which is useful for larger models where you only care about certain components.  
   • TOTA (total results) and AVER (averaged results) are mentioned in the broader schema but are not yet implemented in this RSET table.  
   • For structural plotting of material distribution or “volume elements,” the record type STRU is used, but it belongs to a separate section.  

4. Cross References  
   • For brick element stress histograms generated by non-linear runs, see the BRIC TYPE codes under TALPA/ASE or the DYNA and HYDRA postprocessors.  
   • In multi-case analyses you may combine RSET with AND (logical AND of results) or LC (load-case identifiers) to filter and compare stress output across scenarios.  

This description should enable an automated RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system to index each record unambiguously, link it to its numeric dimension, and understand the broader coordinate and programmatic context without needing to inspect the raw table.

This table defines the first two fields of the RSET (Result Set) record, which is used to collect and identify computed result data—often histograms or structural‐volume values—after various numerical analyses (for example with TALPA/ASE, FEABENCH, DYNA or HYDRA). In the broader context of BRIC data structures (see also AND, LC), additional items such as TOTA and AVER exist but are not yet active. Structure values (e.g. material numbers from record STRU) and BRIC TYPE literals (e.g. “Histograms after a non‐linear calculation…”) are handled elsewhere. Here is how each field works:

1. Item: ID  
   • Description: Unique identifier for this result set.  
   • Unit: LIT4 (a four‐character literal)  
   • Default: “!”  
   • Details:  
     – Every RSET record must carry an ID. This 4-character code gives a concise, human‐readable tag for lookup in post-processing or plotting routines.  
     – If the user does not supply an explicit ID, the system assigns the placeholder “!” to signal an unnamed or temporary result set.  
     – Typical practice is to choose mnemonic IDs (e.g. “HIST”, “STVS”) that reflect the type of data contained.

2. Item: REPR  
   • Description: Type of the representation of the result data. Two literal options:  
       • DIAG – Diagram representation  
       • DLST – Text list  
   • Unit: LIT (an unspecified‐length literal)  
   • Default: “–” (dash)  
   • Details:  
     – REPR tells downstream tools how the data in this result set should be interpreted or formatted.  
     – “DIAG” is used if the record contains data meant for graphical display (e.g. a histogram curve).  
     – “DLST” indicates a plain text listing of values (e.g. raw nodal displacements).  
     – If the field is left blank, the default dash “–” flags that no particular representation has been requested; in such cases, the consumer may apply a generic default or raise an error.

Usage Notes:  
• In an RSET definition, the order of items is fixed: ID must appear before REPR.  
• Future extensions may reactivate fields like TOTA (total values) or AVER (averages) to provide summary statistics automatically.  
• When assembling result sets for BRIC‐type output, match REPR to the post‐processing routines: e.g. choose DIAG if you intend to feed the data into a plotting tool, or DLST if you need a formatted table for reports.  
• Consult the AND (Boolean filters) and LC (load combinator) sections for conditional selection of multiple RSET records.
